The extent to which PPDs of young stars are affected by these processes, however, is still unclear, and a notable example of this phenomenon is the case of TW Hydrae, a low-mass star exhibiting significant outburst activity and strong magnetic fields.  The high-angular resolution capabilities of the Next Generation Very Large Array (ngVLA) will enable precise measurement of the disk's mass loss rate, potentially allowing scientists to distinguish between the effects of photoevaporation and MHD breath models. In multi-group broadcasting systems that utilize millimeter wave (mmWave) technology, the primary concern is data loss due to interference between group-specific beams, limiting the potential performance gains in such scenarios. To overcome this challenge, we introduce a hybrid encoding strategy that adapts to both the specific channel conditions and the number of groups, aiming to optimize overall system performance. In contrast to conventional methods that prioritize minimizing interference, our proposed method instead allocates more power to the main beam and distributes it among weaker beams, achieving better multi-group broadcasting outcomes. Theoretical analysis confirms our approach outperforms existing methods and is applicable in both large and limited antenna settings. Furthermore, simulation results validate our findings and reveal a notable improvement in the case of an unevenly distributed multi-group scenario. Overall, our novel hybrid encoding strategy offers enhanced performance and is a more reliable choice for mmWave multi-group broadcasting systems. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/sammywong1994/hybrid-encoding.

This paper presents an innovative decomposition technique for complex robust optimization problems featuring uncertain variables constrained by binary rules. By utilizing Lagrangian duality in a two-stage approach, we develop computationally efficient and progressively tighter lower bounds for the problem's value, leveraging complete and incomplete conditional complete cuts obtained through C&CP relaxation. These bounds rely on two dual problems: a two-stage Lagrangian dual problem and a Reynolds trilevel problem, with the latter offering tighter bounds initially. Incomplete conditional complete cuts derived from C&CP relaxation are then added as cutting plane constraints to strengthen the Lagrangian dual bounds, enabling us to converge to the exact solution by alternating between optimization of the two-stage problem and Lagrangian duality, with the addition of no-cut and cut-and-join operations. This novel approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, offering up to 9% gap reduction for a variety of test cases in scenarios with ambiguous coefficients. Computational results for an ambiguous version of the stochastic capacitated vehicle routing problem demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in obtaining significantly tighter bounds with a reduced gap compared to previously used methods. Moreover, our approach proves capable of obtaining exact solutions for problems previously intractable, including scenarios featuring 50 nodes, 250 customers, and uncertain parameters constrained by binary rules. Our method's source code is publicly available for download at https://github.com/caoyanwang/LagDual_RBO. Its use requires only standard linear and quadratic programming solvers, with no need for specialized optimization software or branch-and-cut algorithms, making our approach widely accessible to practitioners. The COVID-19 pandemic has led to an alarming surge in global infectious diseases, highlighting the need for rapid and precise epidemiological analysis to inform public policy and emergency response planning.
To address this need, researchers are now employing data analytics and machine learning techniques to track daily COVID infections across various cities worldwide, leveraging open-source surveillance data platforms. 
Despite the availability of real-time epidemiological data, statistical analysis is typically employed to provide delayed insights into disease progression, suggesting a need for more sophisticated, data-driven approaches using intelligent tools for pandemic management and control. 
To bridge this gap, researchers are now creating large, diverse, multi-source, and multi-modal datasets for socioeconomic analysis in urban areas, enabling machine learning models to accurately predict future infectious trends and helping policymakers develop effective strategies for disease prevention and mitigation. 
To this end, we introduce the H4M Dataset, a unique collection of data from Beijing, China, for the purposes of socioeconomic analytics and pandemic management. 
This dataset, comprising 13 distinct sources, includes essential features for predicting and analyzing infectious trends, as well as a range of other valuable information for urban planners and policymakers. 
Using this dataset, we have trained several machine learning models, achieving remarkable accuracy and paving the way for future research and applications. 
Our analysis of the H4M Dataset has significant implications for pandemic management, urban planning, and socioeconomic policy-making in urban areas, making it an invaluable resource for researchers and practitioners in these fields. 
To facilitate further research, we have made the H4M Dataset available for public download at https://github.com/yingxiaoming/H4M-Dataset. 
Researchers can also submit their papers to a special issue on socioeconomic analytics in urban areas for review and consideration. 

The H4M dataset is designed to facilitate socioeconomic analytics and pandemic management in urban areas, consisting of 13 datasets that capture the daily COVID infections across Beijing in 2020. 
This diversity in data sources enables researchers to model various complex urban problems, including but not limited to, sudden-onset epidemic outbreaks. 
Each dataset is rich in features that capture different aspects of the data, including time series, point-of-interest visits, public transportation usage, air quality and weather patterns. 
This diversity in data sources and rich set of features make the H4M dataset a valuable resource for researchers to tackle a range of challenges in machine learning and data analytics. 
Furthermore, the H4M dataset is designed to support not only supervised learning but also transfer learning, semi-supervised learning, and zero-shot learning

The increasing complexity of data management systems' design and the expanding scope of data science have created a need for a more unified approach to supporting both automated reasoning and human exploration. To address this, we are developing a concept called VisiBig, a visual analysis framework that enables the interactive examination of large datasets tied to comprehensive, formal schemata. By integrating automated reasoning and interactive exploration, VisiBig facilitates the discovery of data relationships and entities. Its current implementation incorporates a Big Data Materialized View Cache for supporting interactive exploration and automated reasoning. The effectiveness of this cache is demonstrated through experiments. Further development is also focused on enhancing VisiBuilder, a tool for visually editing and customizing the data schema, and VisiBig's support for query analysis and discovery. As part of this effort, we have created a prototype called VisiBig Investigator, which allows users to explore and investigate big data distributions tied to formal schemata. The results of this work are being applied in a use case involving the Italian National Research Data Catalog. Given the scope of data management, which encompasses big data, research data, and semi-structured text, we believe that VisiBig has the potential to become a general-purpose tool for supporting data analysis and discovery. Given its current limitations, which are primarily related to performance issues and the need for a more user-friendly interface, we consider VisiBig Investigator to be a promising prototype that requires further development to become a fully functional tool. Nevertheless, we believe that even in its current form, VisiBig can serve as an inspiration and a valuable resource for the data management and discovery community. The source code of VisiBig Investigator is publicly available under the MIT license at https://github.com/visibig/. This study focuses on the challenge of learning from limited data for multi-class problems in the scenario where each class contains diverse instances and only a few examples are available. Prior research used global prototypes to model individual classes, but this approach is impractical when dealing with many classes and limited data because it requires precise estimates of mean positions and covariances in each class. To address this issue, we propose the Class-type Prototype Learning framework, which dynamically changes the number of global prototypes based on the actual number of classes and uses a set of learnable, class-type global prototypes to represent multiple classes compactly. Each prototype represents a group of classes with similar characteristics, and a simple assignment mechanism is used to map instances to their corresponding class prototypes. Our framework outperforms other methods in their use of global prototypes on datasets such as CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, both in the setting where data is available for training and in the setting where data is limited. Additionally, our framework achieves better results than state-of-the-art methods on the mini-ImageNet and Stanford 40 Classes datasets both in the setting where data is available for training and in the setting where data is limited. Our framework's source code is available for public use.

This investigation involves analyzing various parameters and parameters of its complement, along with determining the minimum order necessary for such graphs to exist. Additionally, we establish the conditions under which a graph can be converted into its complement, and identify specific graph patterns that cannot be converted. Finally, we take initial steps towards applying these findings to the broader class of chordal graphs. This research contributes essential results towards understanding the unique properties of split graphs and their equivalents, and opens the door for further related investigations. It also sets a benchmark for developing solutions to similar problems in the realm of product graphs. Specifically, we demonstrate that while the product of two split graphs can maintain its semi-transitive property, this is not the case when we consider products with cliques, and that semi-transitivity does not translate to its product with a bipartite graph. This research also sets a new challenge for investigating the properties of product graphs, and the findings will likely have significant implications for further studies in this area. This research outlines a novel method for designing a robust motion planning approach that prioritizes safety and system resilience. By utilizing control barrier functions, we have developed a strategy to create a time-varying level set that can effectively restrict the robot's trajectory to a predetermined space, thereby avoiding dynamic obstacles while minimizing impact from uncertainty effects. Building upon this framework, we present a multi-objective motion planning problem that simultaneously optimizes trajectory speed and a cost function while adhering to three primary objectives: 1) obstacle avoidance, 2) system stability, and 3) overall efficiency. Notably, our approach ensures that these objectives are continuously updated in real-time and that the corresponding system dynamics remain continuous and differentiable. By employing optimization techniques, we have successfully designed a robust motion planning algorithm that can effectively navigate complex environments. This method not only accounts for environmental uncertainties but also enables the robot to adapt to unexpected events in real-time. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the practical application of our approach using a quadrotor testbed, highlighting its ability to execute complex tasks while navigating uncertain environments, as evidenced by the testbed's ability to avoid dynamic obstacles and complete a task in the presence of significant uncertainties and unexpected events. The evolution of deep neural networks through life-like, self-directed learning has garnered significant interest, drawing comparisons to animal development. Similar to animals, these self-evolving networks grow without preconceived notions of their target environment, which can result in them adapting to local data instead of the broader context. This work delves into organic machine learning, exploring its resilience in coping with instances that might mislead or deceive the system. As an example, the team employed a simplified version of the well-known adversarial perturbation concept to test the behavior of a network that had learned the classification of MNIST digits without being explicitly programmed against such manipulations. This investigation highlighted the significance of understanding and addressing the potential for systemic biases in organic machine learning. This research is intended to serve as a foundation for a more comprehensive study on organic machine learning's robustness in the near future. This analysis reveals that the solutions converge towards the corresponding local diffusion equation under two distinct conditions: with or without a background velocity field. The human mind's functional connectivity is defined by interactions between distant brain regions. Current models primarily rely on synchronized neural activity to describe these connections. However, a more comprehensive understanding of human cognition suggests that more than just synchronization alone is involved. We propose an approach to map the functional brain network by accounting for all types of correlations between different brain regions. Our results show that the resulting network structure is more in line with the organization of language and is better at differentiating distinct regions, also demonstrating how damage to the brain can lead to cognitive impairments by disrupting even weakly connected regions. This total association framework for modeling the brain's connectivity offers an important step forward in understanding human cognition. Our research is accessible online at www.totalassociation.org. Users can explore and simulate the brain's connectivity using an interactive tool. Analyzing the total association matrix has also led to the development of several open-source code repositories, which are available on GitHub at https://github.com/totassoc. Additionally, a comprehensive dataset of total association matrices for the human brain is available for download through the University of Colorado Boulder's Data Repository at https://datamove.colorado.edu. We welcome the public to contribute to our research by suggesting new methods for interpreting the total association matrix and improving its associated tools. This paper extends the Segal-Bargmann Hilbert space to a Clifford algebra-valued setting, establishing an isomorphism with a space of homogeneous polynomials defined over the algebra. A new unitary transformation is introduced, linking this space to the one formed by monomials, and it is shown to be a C-star algebra-valued generalization of the traditional Segal-Bargmann transformation. interior and boundary cases, is presented, where the conditioning is expressed
in terms of a Gaussian field's reproducing kernel Hilbert space. This method
involves assigning a measure to the field's realizations and derives a
non-degenerate distribution on the field's index space, enabling pointwise
definition and a direct representation of the conditional distribution. Key
results demonstrate a measure representation of the conditional properties and
a Doléans-Dade exponential for Gaussian field conditioning, facilitating a
unified understanding of this concept. Additionally, this approach yields an
explicit representation of the conditional properties in terms of multi-variable
polynomials, allowing for its practical application in solving stochastic PDEs.

deterministic versions of known results, such as the Karhunen-Loève expansion

pointwise definition of the conditional properties and provides an explicit
representation of the field's values given its restrictions. As a consequence,

In continuous control problems, a widely used actor-critic framework often faces
a common challenge: achieving convergence in off-policy learning. This issue arises
due to the actor's policy adjustments causing samples collected in the past to become
increasingly irrelevant. A notable method, experience replay with ER5, reduces the
variance of the critic target by decoupling it from the actor's policy, but this
approach still leaves approximately 50% of past samples relevant only through their
average, increasing the likelihood of off-policy learning failure. To address this
problem, a new method is proposed that combines ER5 with a dynamic variance decrease
algorithm, allowing the quickest possible reduction in sample variance as conditions
allow, without compromising off-policy data utility. This approach is demonstrated to
significantly accelerate variance decrease, retaining more-off-policy relevant data
and substantially improving the performance of actor-critic algorithms. As such, it is
highly effective when used in conjunction with other methods that enhance off-policy
learning, such as bootstrapping without function approximation. When integrated into
MDP problems, it is shown to surpass ER5 on approximately 80% of environments from
roboschool, while matching its performance in most instances. Furthermore, when used
in combination with actor-critic algorithms that enhance off-policy learning, such as
TD3 and SAC, it is found to enhance their capabilities, with results that are within
human-level performance on challenging control benchmarks like human-level
reinforcement learning. This outcome is a direct consequence of accelerated
off-policy learning, with results that are visually represented on challenging
benchmark problems. The proposed method is available for immediate use through
open-source libraries such as torch-rl. An accompanying video is available at

Certain tiny six-legged insects called springtails are able to move around on water's surface by using their legs to propel themselves forward. Research conducted by the author of the paper observed springtails crawling across a 10 micrometer thick water film at room temperature. It was discovered that the lower the water film's viscosity, the faster the springtails moved. This suggests the presence of high Reynolds numbers in their locomotion dynamics. A theoretical model based on the springtail's body shape was developed to explain the observed movement patterns. It was proposed that the springtails move by using their legs to create ripples in the water film that are amplified behind their body, creating the necessary propulsion to move forward. This mechanism does not rely on the water's surface viscosity and therefore remains effective at low viscosities. This study investigates how the Casimir effect affects thermodynamic properties of a blackbody.  We examined this phenomenon in a previous work and found that, at zero temperature, the presence of two mirrors attached to the blackbody led to a reduction in entropy by the amount of the Casimir entropy.  The current investigation focuses on the non-zero temperature behavior of the Casimir effect and its impact on the heat capacity of the blackbody, which is influenced by the placement of the mirrors.  Interestingly, the heat capacity of the blackbody in the presence of the Casimir effect exhibits characteristics that resemble those of a metal, further supporting the idea that the heat capacity of the heat radiation is not negligible.  Our results demonstrate that the thermodynamic properties of a blackbody are affected by the Casimir effect and that this effect can be observed experimentally through the study of the blackbody's heat capacity.  Furthermore, the study reveals that the heat capacity of the heat radiation, which was previously believed to be negligible, is not negligible and is equal to one-quarter the heat capacity of a metal, which could have a significant impact on our understanding of the heat radiation.  Finally, the study highlights the potential for experimental verification of the Casimir effect by means of blackbody thermometry.  Such an experiment could provide a unique means of confirming the existence of the Casimir effect, which has been demonstrated primarily through theoretical calculations and microwave-based experiments in a range of quantum field theory models.  The potential for experimental verification through blackbody thermometry is particularly significant given the relative ease with which blackbody setups can be constructed compared to the complex equipment required for microwave-based experiments. A significant concern with location tracking is that a person's whereabouts may reveal sensitive information, such as destinations like hospitals, clinics, and places of worship, which should remain private. To address this issue, an individual may choose to reveal fake location data to protect their actual location inquiries. However, an adversary may try to utilize this fake data to infer the genuine location inquiries. In this research, we examine the issue of an adversary limiting a user's location inquiries based on their fake data trails. We present a family of conditional distributions that accommodate diverse prior probabilities over a user's genuine location inquiries. We develop an optimization technique to find the best-in-class fake data trail under any given conditional distribution, which yields better privacy guarantees compared to previous methods. Moreover, our results show that prior distributions do not significantly impact the quality of the fake data trails, which means they can be disregarded when optimizing fake data trails. We also provide a method to evaluate how effective our optimization technique is in safeguarding a user's location inquiries based on their fake data trails. We apply our approach to real-world datasets and demonstrate its effectiveness. The approach can be found on GitHub under the repository 'Location Privacy Under Conditional Distributions'. Additionally, a related paper titled 'Location Privacy Under Conditional Distributions' is posted online at arXiv.

A highly influential field, Autonomous Driving, heavily relies on 3D localization which, despite recent advancements, still faces difficulties with precise localization on large-scale maps. The limitations of current methods stem from their inability to efficiently process global maps and adapt to environmental changes. To address these challenges, a novel localization approach, NDT-Transformer, is proposed. This method transforms 3D point clouds into Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) depictions and represents them as sequential images, facilitating the processing of large-scale maps. A novel transformer-based network, NDT-Transformer, is developed to align and compare these depictions, and its effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on publicly available datasets. The results show that NDT-Transformer outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly in loop closures and large-scale localization scenarios. Additionally, the source code and related datasets are publicly available for further research.

Typically, two-Higgs-doublet models are evaluated separately due to distinct constraints from their tree-level properties, which often conflict with other data. A global minimization of the Higgs potential enables us to calculate physical properties, such as the masses of the Higgs bosons and $W$ and $Z$ gauge bosons. Our findings show that with purely real parameters, two-Higgs-doublet models cannot satisfy multiple constraints simultaneously. In contrast, allowing complex parameters resolves some inconsistencies, enabling model compatibility with various data, including within the $2\sigma$ range for mass spectra similar to the Standard Model. Our analysis includes physical decays like $\tau^+\tau^-$ and $bb$, as well as less commonly considered processes like radiative $b\rightarrow s$ transitions involving Majorana neutrinos. Our analysis assumes Standard Model-like couplings and does not consider additional constraints from precision electroweak data or cosmological observations. Nevertheless, incorporating these data could further restrict two-Higgs-doublet model parameters. Our analysis assumes a two-Higgs-doublet model with two distinct Yukawa interactions, one primarily coupling to $b$-quarks and a second coupling to lighter quarks. However, our conclusions may be applicable to other two-Higgs-doublet models with similar tree-level properties. Despite the effectiveness of supervised training in this field, the quality of the training data significantly impacts performance, particularly when dealing with noisy labels obtained from search logs. To improve document ranking despite label noise, we propose a two-stage approach that employs bag sampling and cluster-wise loss to mitigate noise and enhance model robustness. Next, the model is reweighted to minimize the influence of noisy labels, with loss recalculated on a per-cluster basis to maximize relevance. The Indian Space Research Organisation is developing a space telescope called the INSIST mission, which is being considered for execution in the Astrosat-2 mission stage. This new telescope will focus on understanding Black Holes, Neutron Stars, and X-ray binaries by allowing for in-depth spectral analysis of weak X-ray sources that currently cannot be studied due to limitations of existing ground-based telescopes. 

Key INSIST mission objectives include examining the characteristics of stellar mass Black Holes and Neutron Stars in multiple environments, investigating the nature of Low-Mass X-ray Binaries, and collecting essential data on Low-Intensity Active Galactic Nuclei. Furthermore, the telescope will aid in the creation of detailed maps of the Galactic Soft X-ray background, an essential step in understanding the nature of this unexplained phenomenon. 

If executed, INSIST will become India's second high-resolution X-ray space-based observatory, following the launch of the AstroSat satellite which carries the Cadmium-Zinc-Telluride Spectroscopic Imager. This new telescope will surpass the CCD imager's capabilities, enabling clearer observations of weak sources and their emission spectra. Key INSIST characteristics include an energy range spanning from 0.1 to 10 keV, a resolution of 50 eV at this energy range, and a field of view of 1.3 x 1.3 square degrees. 

This paper summarises the proposed INSIST telescope and presents the outcomes of a recently completed technology demonstration program. During this program, an INSIST prototype was tested in a laboratory setting to verify its performance in real-world conditions. This testing confirmed that INSIST can achieve the desired resolution and collect detailed X-ray spectra within the 0.1 to 10 keV energy range. 
Key INSIST features include an energy resolution of 50 eV at specific energy levels and around 70 eV across the entire 0.1 to 10 keV range, and a pixel response uniformity of around 5% along with high quantum efficiency across the same energy range. 
These results validate the INSIST concept and confirm its suitability for execution in the Astrosat-2 mission stage.

We define topologically generated groups as groups whose topological properties are determined by a specific subset of their free topological modules over a given rational vector space. We prove that every such group, being topologically free, can be represented as a subset of a free topological vector space. We further demonstrate that the family of topologically free groups, being topologically free, is closed under a range of operations including arbitrary intersections and unions. We establish that the standard framework functor, mapping any topologically free group to its corresponding free topological vector space, provides a equivalence of categories between $\mathcal{G}$ and the category of free topological vector spaces. We show that this functor, being dense, has a key implication: the existence of certain invariants unique to topologically free groups is shown to be equivalent to the existence of invariants unique to free topological vector spaces. We identify specific invariants, namely, cardinalities of intersections and unions, that hold for all topologically free groups. We generalize these findings to the broader context of standard framework spaces, which encompass various types of topological groupoids, quandles, and other mathematical structures. Notably, we identify specific invariants, namely, cardinalities of intersections and unions, that hold for all standard framework spaces. We further demonstrate that these invariants can be characterized through the lens of a novel combinatorial structure, known as the difference graph. We show that the cardinalities of intersections and unions of any two distinct points in a free framework space are encoded in the maximum sizes of certain types of connected components in the corresponding difference graph. We prove a sufficient condition for the existence of such connected components, thereby establishing a framework for the study of combinatorial problems with implications in framework topology. This led to a partition of the set I(E,3) of such subsets into disjoint blocks, each labeled as a three-element subset, with a natural ordering. This division of I(E,3) can be seen as a outer algebra over the set {0, 1, 2,..., n-1} with coefficients in {0, 1}, with a defined operation based on the 3-rank relation. This paper examines the outer algebra's properties and its connections to the set's linear independence, the presence of rank-one elements, the characteristic series, and the concept of rank-one independence in matroids. It also explores how these properties are related to each other, as well as how they can be used to determine whether a given three-element subset is an independent set in a given matroid. Additionally, this paper defines a binary operation, known as the hyperproduct, between two three-element subsets, and investigates its properties and relationships. It also uses computer algorithms to calculate the outer algebras for sets with at most eight elements, and presents examples of these algebras for various values of three-element subsets. Finally, this paper discusses potential areas of research and future work related to the outer algebras in matroid theory. Active learning strategies for reducing dialogue system training data costs advocate for strategically selecting and labeling uncertain interactions. To enhance monitoring models' accuracy, labeling topologically dependent interactions is crucial. This work investigates the uncertainty sources affecting predictive models, focusing on the role of ASR uncertainty in enhancing monitoring capabilities. By representing ASR uncertainty as a confusion network, labeling tools are developed to integrate it into a DSM model, enabling the identification of sensitive interactions to changes in ASR output. This is achieved by utilizing Levenshtein edit distance and surface-level features derived from the Confusion Network. An ASR module with built-in uncertainty is integrated into a DSDS framework, comparing its performance with a counterpart assuming a reliable ASR output. Experimental results on the MIT Bankteller dataset demonstrate that ASR uncertainty significantly impacts dialogue system performance, with a marginally improved performance when uncertainty is considered. This outcome suggests that strategic ASR uncertainty selection for labeling can yield better results than topologically dependent selection. Moreover, ASR uncertainty is a crucial factor that should not be overlooked when designing interactions for labeling under an active learning framework. This research is the first to incorporate ASR uncertainty into DSDS models, paving the way for the development of uncertainty-aware interaction selection methods. Automated program repair is a rapidly evolving field focused on finding repairs for bugs in software. Current repair approaches typically generate a single repair candidate at a time, using a trial-and-error strategy to achieve high precision. However, this strategy can be problematic when multiple repair candidates coexist with bugs. To address this issue, we introduce antagonistic patch creation, a novel technique for generating multiple repair candidates simultaneously. By producing patches that counteract each other, APC ensures all generated patches are valid repairs. We evaluate APC on 1,820 natural bugs from eight diverse software systems and compare its performance with six state-of-the-art repair tools. Results show APC repairs approximately 71% bugs, outperforming the baseline repair tools by 44%. Notably, APC achieves a 100% success rate in repairing bugs introduced as part of two open challenges in on-line coding contests. We also showcase APC's effectiveness in increasing the test coverage of repair candidates. Overall, our research indicates APC is a versatile repair technique capable of producing multiple repair candidates in parallel, offering promising avenues for further research. A major obstacle in robotic learning has been the scarcity of quality training data. To address this challenge, researchers have been seeking high-quality datasets to drive various tasks, including robotic grasping. Currently, existing grasp datasets are limited in scope, often tailored to specific robots or domains, and lack comprehensive object coverage. As a result, reliable grasp policies cannot be effectively transferred to diverse robots and environments. To overcome this limitation, a new robotic grasping dataset, called DexGraspNet, has been developed. This extensive dataset is uniquely designed to facilitate robust grasp planning on a wide range of objects across multiple robotic platforms. Comprising over 1 million simulated robotic states, DexGraspNet surpasses existing datasets in size and generalizability. To enhance its scope, multiple algorithms were employed to improve grasp pose prediction. A novel data-driven approach was also introduced to identify and mitigate biases in grasp pose estimation, thereby enabling accurate grasp planning on real-world objects. Experimental evaluations across three robotic platforms, including Franka Emika, UR5, and Kuka LBR, demonstrate the superior performance of DexGraspNet over existing datasets. Notably, its grasping success rate of 0.2081 is significantly higher than that of the top-performing dataset. The primary goal of knowledge distillation is to facilitate model compression by transferring knowledge from complex models to more compact ones. However, the majority of distillation methods focus on matching the output classification distribution of the teacher and student models without considering data flow. As a result, teacher models often produce intermediate features that cannot be matched by the student models, making it difficult to compress models with multiple convolutional layers. In this context, we introduce InDistill, a unique distillation method that preserves data flow to enable the compression of deep models. InDistill extracts features from the teacher model at specific data-flow aligned layers and conveys this information to the student model through a novel alignment process. This approach enables the student model to replicate those features and facilitates the compression of deep models. Our experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet datasets show that InDistill outperforms existing distillation methods by a significant margin, particularly for models with multiple convolutional layers. For instance, the ResNet-50 model compressed using InDistill achieves a top-1 accuracy of 78.1% on the ImageNet dataset, surpassing existing state-of-the-art distillation methods. The source code for InDistill is publicly available at https://github.com/asharakeh/indistill. We have developed a topological comparison metric for smooth functions defined within a bounded area of the two-dimensional plane, focusing on situations where these functions exhibit linear characteristics. Additionally, a topological comparison metric has been developed for the foliations created by these smooth, linear-like functions. A "nearness" condition, analogous to Lipschitz regularity, is defined using these metrics, and its properties for a single function are thoroughly explored and proven to be equivalent to the "nearness" condition defined using foliation leaves. Furthermore, the notion of "nearness" for multiple functions is extended and it is demonstrated that "nearness" of multiple functions is equivalent to the "nearness" of their individual foliations and foliation leaves. A dimension formula is also derived for the space of smooth, linear-like functions and their foliations. Finally, a local invariance theorem is developed for "nearness" conditions, and key properties including "nearness" of parametrization methods are investigated. The results obtained are potentially applicable to a range of applications, including control theory and differential equations. The concepts and methods employed in this research can be extended to cover situations involving hyperbolic characteristics. A comprehensive list of open questions is provided in the concluding section. This research provides the theoretical foundation for a formal regular approximation method for topological comparison metrics in situations involving smooth, linear-like functions. The well-known CountSketch algorithm utilizes randomized linear measurements to efficiently recover frequently occurring elements within high-dimensional vectors, specifically those containing $\polylog n$ non-negligible non-majority components at scale $n$. It achieves this by utilizing $\polylog n$ random projections, but under adaptive selection, its performance significantly degrades, requiring $n^{1/2 - \Omega()}$ measurements to guarantee frequency recovery. In this study, we re-examine CountSketch's resilience to adversarial selection of dimensions for the non-majority components, demonstrating that under adversarial choice, even with $n^{1/2 - \Omega(1)}$ measurements, it may fail to accurately recover the frequencies, potentially returning wrong vectors with confidence $1 - \Omega(()$. Our work also shows that CountSketch can still maintain near-optimal recovery for majority components under adversarial dimension selection, highlighting a significant distinction between non-majority and majority components. Furthermore, we provide evidence that this adverse performance of CountSketch is an intrinsic limitation, as modifying the algorithm results in comparable frequency recovery guarantees for majority components. However, for non-majority components, improved guarantees come at the cost of substantial algorithmic modifications and a significant increase in required measurements to $n^{1/2 + \Omega(1)}$. In the process, we introduce a novel technique that enables biased sketching for non-majority components, a problem of ongoing discussion in the information theory literature. Specifically, we establish the existence of skewed skewed-sketchs that can effectively capture biased, skewed frequency information using only $n^{1/2 + \Omega(1)}$ measurements. Interestingly, we show that this novel class of sketches does not directly imply the existence of optimal, unbiased ones. Ultimately, we speculate that the existence of optimal, unbiased CountSketch might require a different approach, as the current understanding suggests it would require significantly more than $n^{1/2}$ measurements to accurately recover the frequencies, likely indicating that such a sketch might be impossible to create. A fundamental aspect of robotic control, structural integrity is essential for any task. For complex missions involving multiple robots, maintaining structural stability across all agents is crucial. This paper introduces Simultaneous Robotic Structure (SRS), a novel control method for coordinating multi-robot teams on a single, rigid structure. Leveraging an external force sensor on one robot to sense the others, SRS utilizes a local Jacobian observer to estimate the structure's state, achieving state estimation within 10% of the actual state. This allows the team to perform a series of challenging tasks, such as picking and placing objects, while maintaining structural stability, all without relying on external sensing or virtualization. With a focus on multi-robot systems, SRS showcases its superiority over single-robot systems using a similar sensor. This innovative control method demonstrates the potential for multiple robots working in tandem on a single structure, via an experiment where two 6-DoF robots perform a picking and placing task, resulting in a success rate of 98%. Additionally, SRS is applied to a quadrotor swarm, successfully completing a challenging object-picking task among a group of 4 robots. This work showcases SRS's capabilities in various complex robotic scenarios, paving the way for a broad range of applications. A comprehensive video demonstrating SRS is available at https://youtu.be/6jzgqk0wq6I. The code for SRS is available at https://github.com/asharakeh/Simultaneous_Robotic_Structure. Recent studies suggest that self-supervised learning can be more effective than supervised methods for certain tasks. We investigate whether depth estimation pre-training leads to improved performance in semantic segmentation, and whether this benefit varies depending on the employed depth estimation method. To answer this, we introduce a novel pre-training approach that utilizes a multi-task loss, separating surface points into static structures and dynamic objects. Our results show that pre-training on the COLMAP static object dataset enhances semantic segmentation performance, particularly when using a column-based surface representation. Notably, our low-complexity static object estimator can run in under 0.1 seconds and uses less than 0.5 GB of RAM on average, making it a suitable choice for resource-constrained devices. Overall, our study indicates that depth estimation pre-training offers advantages over traditional classification-based pre-training in semantic segmentation tasks. In a regular triangular lattice, when three distinct Delaunay triangles share a single vertex, two more triangles are formed, each sharing no vertices with the initial one. This concept is illustrated and a proof demonstrated, primarily utilizing a visual and intuitive approach that relies on basic geometric principles. Although the proof does not follow the traditional structure of a mathematical argument, it effectively conveys the idea by avoiding reliance on high-level assumptions about non-degenerate triangles in a triangular lattice. The underlying assumption that at least three such triangles exist in the lattice is implicit, but does not need to be explicitly stated. Ultimately, this simple yet elegant idea highlights the unique characteristics of a triangular lattice and its distinct features compared to other types of lattices. A key insight arising from this concept is that any set of two or three distinct Delaunay triangles in a regular triangular lattice defines a subset of four Delaunay triangles, and this subset forms a geometric pattern that can be characterized as a tetrahedron. This notion is analogous to the concept of a shell of triangles in a regular grid, but one that is unique to triangular lattices due to their inherent properties. A more formal and rigorous proof of the idea is also provided, but it is noted that the original demonstration is more accessible and easier to understand for those familiar with the subject. In a broader context, this concept is connected to the broader field of geometric shell theorems, and it is hoped that this simple yet powerful idea may inspire further discussion and analysis among mathematicians and non-mathematicians alike. Graph neural networks have demonstrated impressive performance across a range of applications. However, integrating them into a larger system proves to be a complex and difficult task, largely due to the lack of suitable general frameworks. This challenge is compounded by the diverse set of input/outputs and operations supported by GNNs. To address this issue, we propose the Graph Neural Network Interpreter, a flexible framework that enables the dynamic configuration of GNN models through a standardized template. This approach allows for the easy adaptation of various GNN models, multiple input/outputs, and different operation sets. Furthermore, we developed a parameterized interpreter for the Python implementation of GNNs, facilitating the testing and evaluation of our framework. The proposed interpreter has been successfully applied to multiple benchmark GNN models, achieving comparable results to manually implemented versions. This framework is expected to significantly aid the development of tools, tools chains, and workflows for GNNs, serving as a fundamental utility for the community. This research outlines a model-driven reinforcement learning approach that utilizes explanation mechanisms. The goal is to have a pre-existing model that can explain its decision-making processes, ultimately leading to the discovery of a solution strategy. In this study, we employed Inductive Logic Programming to create an experiential environment and a learner that can replicate the model's behavior. The model's state transition and reward policies were developed using traditional machine learning techniques, but the generated programs cannot be interpreted as to why they were implemented in that manner. To rectify this, we integrated an ILP system, which allows the program to include logical explanations regarding its decision-making processes. The proposed framework was tested on two complex problems: the design of optimal bin distributions and the sequential assembly of large structures. While the model-driven ILP approach was successful in these domains, it faced issues with efficiency due to its computationally intensive nature. This problem may be mitigated through data augmentation techniques, which are presented as potential solutions. The proposed model-driven ILP framework offers a new approach to the exploration of the reinforcement learning problem and highlights its potential as a method for uncovering the underlying causes of machine learning models. The research indicates that, with further refinement, this method could be used to develop more transparent and explainable reinforcement learning algorithms. Ultimately, this could lead to increased trust in these models, particularly in high-stakes industries. Blind image restoration, specifically blind deblurring/denoising, aims to clear a image that has been smudged due to a known or unknown blur effect/ noise level. The challenge lies in finding an optimal image that not only visually makes sense but also mathematically fits the observed blurred image. Prior research often made initial estimates about the image quality or blur effect/ noise level before the restoration process. However, these assumptions aren't always necessary, and the image can be restored without them - referred to as the blind case. 

In this research, a new blind image restoration approach is presented, where a mixture of convolution kernels and total variation regularization is used. The image is split into non-blurred regions, where a clear image estimate is formed, and the blur effect is applied to create a blurred image. A linear combination of low-rank and sparse convolution kernels is used to create the blur effect model, with the rank and sparsity weights being estimated as well. 

Experiments show that this new approach produces high quality results, even when there are irregular shaped boundaries, missing data, and the depth of the image layers is unknown. The estimated image and blur effect parameters are visually inspected to ensure they make sense in the context of the restored image. The research's source code is available online to facilitate future research.

Formal verification of programs typically relies on pre and post conditions expressed through first-order logic statements. This research introduces a new approach called Natural Hoare Reasoning, which uses more expressive first-order logic statements based on phrases in natural language, allowing for easier specification of programs without the constraints of formal languages. Our method translates natural language descriptions into these statements using a formal grammar and then verifies the program against it, enabling even less formal descriptions to ensure program correctness. This innovative technique enables the automatic transformation of natural language specifications into high-level programming language statements, paving the way for a more accessible formal verification process. Although still in its initial phase, our experiments show promising results and highlight several challenges that need to be overcome to make this approach practical. This study marks an important step in integrating natural language specifications with formal verification, opening up new possibilities for a more declarative programming model. Haskell allows for concise and efficient code with its functional nature, complementing the development of the parsing logic through the use of monads and list processing capabilities. Distributed consensus is a fundamental process that enables coordinated activity in a distributed system. Researchers have thoroughly examined the subject in a setting with failovers, focusing particularly on how block creation and distribution impact system architecture. Although extensive research exists, there is a lack of consensus-building solutions that can adapt to failures and diverse types of errors without relying on specific assumptions about network topology or the behavior of faulty components. This study addresses the challenge of achieving consensus in a distributed setting with multiple failures and diverse types of errors. A novel flow control protocol called Canopus has been proposed, demonstrating the potential for a distributed system to reach an agreement on a shared ledger. Building on this foundation, we present RCanopus, a Canopus variant designed to withstand multiple failures and diverse types of errors. RCanopus achieves this by leveraging a specialized failure detection mechanism, reducing the probability of errors through a more efficient flow control mechanism, and utilizing a unique feature to prevent errors caused by non-failure-related failures. A formal proof confirms that RCanopus achieves the required properties of a consensus-building protocol, and our experiments show that RCanopus outperforms Canopus in terms of agreement probability. This advantage holds even in scenarios with multiple failures and diverse types of errors. A prototype implementation of RCanopus has been developed and tested against Canopus. Experimental results confirm that RCanopus performs better in terms of agreement probability and latency compared to Canopus. Furthermore, our experiments show that RCanopus remains stable under diverse failure patterns and diverse types of errors. A newly proposed Bayesian method called BayesOD for object detectors demonstrates the importance of uncertainty quantification in deep learning. By incorporating prior knowledge into its model, a Bayesian deep learning model can effectively evaluate its own reliability. However, creating a Bayesian object detector that accurately reflects the true state of the world is a complex task, as object priors must balance the realities of both rare and common objects in the given environment. To address this challenge, we developed two types of priors for a state-of-the-art object detector, enabling it to accurately predict its own uncertainty levels. Experimental results demonstrate that our Bayesian method outperforms its non-Bayesian counterpart and accurately estimates object detection uncertainties on multiple benchmark datasets. The method's source code is publicly available at https://github.com/whwu/BayesOD.git.  In the future, we plan to further refine our Bayesian object detector to provide more precise and reliable uncertainty assessments. Specifically, we will focus on refining the object detection priors to more effectively capture various real-world scenarios. Ultimately, we aim to develop a robust and reliable uncertainty model for deep object detectors, facilitating their safe deployment in real-world applications. A potential extension of this work is the development of a Bayesian semi-supervised object detector, enabling it to effectively learn from both labeled and unlabeled data. By creating a robust uncertainty model for object detection, we can help mitigate the adverse effects of adversarial attacks on object detectors, enabling them to accurately identify and counter potential threats in the given environment. Specifically, we can use our Bayesian object detector to detect and evade adversarial examples that are intentionally designed to mislead object detectors. A potential future work in this area involves the development of a robust and reliable uncertainty model for object detection that can effectively counter adversarial attacks, even those that arise from unintended sources such as camera noise and environmental changes. To achieve this goal, we can use our Bayesian object detector to predict its own uncertainty levels and develop a countermeasure for adversarial examples that can effectively limit their ability to cause harm. This work presents an traffic forecasting system called TrafficInsight. It provides point-of-interest (POI)-based traffic forecasting by analyzing moving segments of traffic. These moving segments, defined as large clusters of low-speed vehicles, serve as indicators of traffic conditions. By utilizing these moving segments and associated POI data, TrafficInsight generates short-term traffic forecasts, up to 2 hours in advance, based on spatio-temporal Markov chains. These chains model the probability of moving segments and associated POI activities at discrete time intervals. To demonstrate the effectiveness of TrafficInsight, it is applied to real-world traffic data collected from highways in Seoul, South Korea. By analyzing this data, researchers identified that traffic moving segments are often associated with recurring events like rush hour and road maintenance. Furthermore, these moving segments tend to maintain consistent speeds along routes. Results from validation tests show that TrafficInsight achieves an error rate of 16.9% for forecasting traffic conditions 30 minutes in advance. However, there is still room for improvement in enhancing the accuracy of longer-term forecasts, such as those beyond a 30-minute horizon. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to the development of smart transportation systems by enabling effective traffic forecasting for smart cities. We establish a specific ordering, denoted as $\rightarrow_{gr}$, on oriented rewrite graphs, where the equivalence relation $ \equiv_{gr} $ represents the closure of multiple reductions. Notably, $ \rightarrow_{gr} $ can be computed in a polynomial time for graphs with a limited degree. This study derives necessary and sufficient conditions for $\equiv_{gr}$ to result in a consistent ordering, using the concept of multiple connectivity in graph theory. It is also proven that the number of equivalences $ \equiv_{gr} $ exceeds the square root of the number of reductions $\rightarrow_{gr}$, with both values growing polynomially. These findings have implications for the well-foundedness and consistency of Terese's rewriting systems. In particular, a graph is considered well-founded if it meets the requirement that $ \rightarrow_{gr} $ is terminating. On the other hand, a rewriting system is consistent if its $\rightarrow_{gr}$ ordering is well-founded. The current research demonstrates that the number of Gray pairs plays a crucial role in determining the consistency of both oriented and non-oriented rewriting systems. This study also sheds light on the relationship between the system's size and its potential for being consistent in the $gr$-ordering. In addition, a large set of Terese's rewriting systems, denoted as $R_{Ter}^{(n,d)}$, is introduced to facilitate the analysis of the consistency problem, where $n$ represents the size and $d$ the degree of the graph. This is achieved by combining the concepts of Terese's and the monadic partial order principles. Notably, for a specific subset of the $R_{Ter}^{(n,d)}$ systems, the number of Gray pairs can be calculated in polynomial time, thus establishing a lower bound on the size of the smallest consistent ordering, where these systems consistently terminate. Ultimately, the study presents a dichotomy theorem for the $R_{Ter}^{(n,d)}$ systems, where the size of the smallest consistent ordering grows either polynomially or doubly exponentially, depending on the value of $d$, with the latter indicating a loss of computability in the ordering. A multi-layered brain called the hippocampus, crucial for memory formation, is particularly vulnerable to neurological disorders, making its study with hippocampus-based methods essential for diagnosis and treatment of related diseases. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), widely used for hippocampus detection, have limitations in differentiating hippocampus regions, leading to inconsistent results. This study proposes an improved CNN model with partitioned hippocampus representation to support hippocampus detection and hippocampus-based methods in epilepsy and Alzheimer's disease research. An experimental dataset of hippocampus images with health or lesions was used to test the model's effectiveness, demonstrating better performance on classification tasks for each of the three stages (amygdala, cornu ammonis 1, and cornu ammonis 3). The proposed model has implications for automatic hippocampus detection in brain MRI scans. An associated MATLAB code is available for peer review at https://doi.org/10.21249/2022.arCIV.23465.legacy661. Additionally, a GitHub repository at https://github.com/tungtungtungtung/hippocampus_infer_MCNN provides the necessary information for replication and distribution. This research contributes to the advancement of hippocampus detection with partitioned representation in CNNs, enhancing the accuracy of hippocampus-based methods in neuroscience and neurology applications. However, their application in mobile networks is hindered by their limitations. This research introduces a novel, multi-stage image partitioning model that not only captures image features but also reconstructs the image using different types of data, including sparse, fractal, wavelet, and mixed media. The model's objectives are twofold: Firstly, they promote image characteristics such as fractals, color consistency, and sparsity. Secondly, they minimize dissimilarities between image segments. Each stage builds upon the previous one, with the number of image segments adjustable, while constrained by an image dissimilarity minimization term. Due to its complexity, with multiple local minima and non-differentiable functions, we developed an efficient optimization algorithm using Geman-Chan relaxation. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through both synthetic and real-world image experiments. The results show that our model outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of visual quality and objective metrics. Our proposed approach addresses the challenge of ensuring that graph node representations captured by node classification models are free from bias and inclusive. We observed that models like GraphSAGE, which uses a local sampling method for node representation, often learns node characteristics that perpetuate human-bias. We found that this bias is not present in models like DeepWalk and Node2Vec, which use a broader range of nodes in their training. We discovered that models like GraphSAGE can learn bias-free node representations if trained with a larger and more diverse set of nodes. Notably, models trained under our diversity-aware graph reconstruction method with a neighborhood size of at least 11 showed significant improvement in fairness and accuracy compared to other reconstruction methods. Furthermore, we developed a new reconstruction method called LCF, which constrains node representations to be similar within fair subgroups while maintaining accuracy. This approach ensures that neighborhood structures within subgroups are preserved, resulting in fair and accurate node representations. Our experiments show that LCF outperforms existing methods in both fairness and accuracy metrics. Additionally, we found that LCF's localized constraints have a limited impact on model performance, making it a suitable choice for real-world applications. We also introduced a new metric called Localized Fairness, which penalizes reconstruction methods for introducing unfairness into node neighborhoods, and showed that LCF achieves the best results under this constraint. Importantly, we found that LCF's improved fairness comes without a significant trade-off in accuracy, and actually enhances model performance for certain tasks. For instance, our experiments show that LCF achieves better overall F1-score on Amazon Computers and Wikipedia datasets. We also observed similar improvements on other datasets, including IMDB, Blogcatalog, and CiteSeer. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/asharakeh/graph-learning-with-localized-community-fairness. Our paper highlights the importance of fairness in node representation learning, and shows that simple techniques like diversity-aware training and localized graph reconstruction can lead to substantial improvements in fairness and accuracy. We also identify areas for further research, including the need to develop more advanced reconstruction methods that incorporate fairness at the task-level, and to study the impact of fairness on different machine learning tasks and data distributions. Financial market bubbles can be identified by assessing whether market participants' forecasting expectations align with actual outcomes. A novel method for detecting bubbles involves examining the discrepancy between the logarithmic expected termination time of an investment and its actual completion time. Prior studies on bubble detection using logarithmic expectations have assumed investments would reach their goals as intended or, alternatively, would suddenly collapse at an unexpected point of maximum speculation. This study presents a more realistic model in which investments follow a random course towards a expected conclusion. A key finding from this research is that the proposed random expected termination time model outperforms existing solutions in diagnosing bubbles and is more resilient in differentiating between various types of time distributions. Analysis of financial data from the years 2007-2010 further demonstrates the model's effectiveness, showing that the proposed method successfully detects the 2008-2009 financial bubble in line with real-world outcomes. A secondary benefit of this research is that the proposed methods can be executed using minimal computational resources, with a notable time complexity of O(n log^3n) and a memory complexity of O(n). This study's findings have significant practical implications for investors, highlighting the need for caution when investing in markets characterized by unusually high volatility. We've developed a method to calculate the real-time propagator of a driven quantum harmonic oscillator using path integrals, which doesn't rely on saddle-point approximations. Our approach is flexible and can be used to analyze complex driving potentials. By applying the scalar identity in path integrals, we break down the propagator into manageable components, each associated with a localized quantum harmonic oscillator. These sub-oscillators have unique properties such as frequencies, amplitudes, and phases, which determine the propagator's associated term. By simulating the sub-oscillators separately, we use Markov-Chain Monte Carlo techniques to estimate the propagator. Our results show high accuracy in the high driving regime and we compare them with existing literature. We also discuss the practical limitations of our approach due to its complex phase-space distribution of frequencies, amplitudes, and phases. Nevertheless, we believe that our path-integral method offers a valuable framework for studying non-equilibrium quantum harmonic oscillators, even when modified versions like the Lévy-Oscillator are involved. Furthermore, we've established a connection between the imaginary time and the propagator's sign structure, which holds significant potential for understanding non-equilibrium quantum harmonic oscillator dynamics in the absence of a driving force. Review-based product recommendation is a crucial component of modern e-commerce platforms, enabling platforms to streamline navigation and boost sales by presenting users with suggested products based on their search queries. However, the task is complex due to the dual nature of review data, comprising informative textual content and rating values. While text provides semantic descriptions relevant to user queries, knowing the associated ratings is essential for inferring user preferences. To address this challenge, this paper introduces an Interactive Fused Network (SIFN) capable of modeling complex relationships between review texts and their accompanying ratings. Additionally, an ablation study reveals the significant contributions of two proposed sub-modules: a Sentiment-sensitive Module and an Interactive Fusion Module. This research presents a demand-side management strategy that utilizes collective game theory to manage peak electricity demand during periods of high energy prices. A demand model based on energy consumption patterns is used to simulate consumers' energy usage in response to various price scenarios. Each consumer adjusts its usage to maximize profits through a collective game approach, resulting in an equilibrium energy demand profile. Our method offers increased energy savings and higher revenue gains for participants compared to traditional time-of-use pricing schemes. Additionally, the study examines the impact of various factors, including the number of consumers, their initial price assumptions, and the complexity of the demand model on the resulting outcomes. A real-time load charging mechanism is also proposed to ensure the existence of a Nash equilibrium, making it a practical solution for real-world applications. Experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of the approach using actual UK energy consumption data and peak pricing tariffs are presented. Furthermore, the study highlights the potential for collective action among consumers to shape public policy and influence the energy market. In summary, the proposed demand-side management strategy offers a viable solution for coordinating individual energy demands to reduce peak loads and reap greater revenue gains during periods of high electricity prices. In this context, the study offers a valuable contribution to the research on demand-side management and energy market modeling. We found that for black strings in arbitrary dimensions with a single non-zero baryon number, a non-zero baryon number can prevent complete black string collapse, and Hawking radiation may still occur, but its temperature will be higher than in Einstein's theory, particularly for black strings in two dimensions, where a Hawking temperature can be achieved even with a baryon number of one. Additionally, we found that gravitational effects can shift the phase boundary where the black string's imaginary surface where the horizon forms, and Hawking radiation may still occur even if the black string has a negative charge. However, we found some scenarios where the imaginary surface does not intersect the observer's line of sight, indicating Hawking radiation is not possible in those cases. Furthermore, we found that Hawking radiation may still occur, even if the black string has a negative mass, provided the baryon number is sufficiently high, and the negative mass does not hinder radiation emission in those scenarios. However, we found some restrictions on Hawking radiation due to the Rastall theory's modification of Newton's constant, which may affect the stability of charged black string solutions. In summary, our research demonstrates that gravitational and extrinsic volume modifications can influence Hawking radiation, particularly from charged black string solutions, which may exhibit Hawking-like behavior even in two-dimensional spacetime. This paper examines the properties of metrics used to measure the morphological complexity of languages. It investigates the correlations among different metrics, including correlations between metrics from the same language, and compares language-based metrics to metrics derived from typological characteristics. A combined metric is proposed, and its validity is established through both statistical and lexical-based tests. Results show that high complexity languages have lower lexical densities, fewer unique parts of speech, and lower entropy values compared to languages of lower complexity. Consequently, a new combined metric is developed, defined as the product of lexical density and entropy, normalized by unique parts of speech ratio. This metric exhibits strong validation in distinguishing languages of high and low complexity across multiple measures, including syllable density, word density, type-token ratio, and entropy. It demonstrates significant correlations with corpus-based metrics from the same language, and its classification performance is consistent with typological characteristics, including number of prefixes and suffixes, agglutination score, and fusion types. Notably, languages of high complexity have longer word lengths and higher entropy values compared to languages of lower complexity. However, the classification results show that languages of high complexity can be misassigned by the metric in specific language families, including Slavic languages. Overall, the findings suggest that a combination of multiple metrics provides the most comprehensive picture of a language's morphological complexity. The study also highlights potential issues with individual metrics, including those based on word length and phonological complexity. Lastly, the results emphasize the importance of considering both typological characteristics and empirical data when developing and interpreting complexity metrics. While the two approaches may converge in some instances, they yield distinct outcomes, and a comprehensive understanding of language complexity cannot be achieved through either alone. The proposed combined metric offers a solution to this dilemma, and its validity establishes a new standard for classifying languages based on morphological complexity. We analyze a class of elliptic equations where the diffusion coefficient is positive, coupled with a nonnegative, bounded, and weakly differentiable measure defined on the boundary of a domain Ω. This framework assumes a zero boundary Neumann condition and a zero integral of the measure on the boundary. Under specific smallness and regularity constraints on the diffusion coefficient and the measure, we prove the local and classical well-posedness of the associated boundary-value problem for measures supported on sets of positive dimension. Moreover, we establish the well-posedness of the same boundary-value problem for measures supported on one-dimensional sets under even more general conditions. This work draws upon ideas from the theory of Stokes equations and reflects on its connections with recent findings, particularly regarding the determination of surface energies by varifold methods. Lastly, we explore the asymptotic behavior of solutions as the measure vanishes and discuss its implications in this context. Additionally, we provide two specific applications: a regularity result concerning measures supported on one-dimensional sets with vanishing regularity at the boundary, and an analysis of a free-boundary problem involving a free surface described by a measure supported on a level set. These applications are rooted in a variational context related to a recent result by Junho Calatroni. Finally, further research directions are proposed. Moreover, relevant findings were shared during seminars at the University of Pisa in 2020 and at the University of Brescia in 2021. In graph theory, an upward planar drawing is a type of planar drawing where all angles are positive, which means that when looking at any vertex, the adjacent edges to the right lie to the right, while those to the left do. This concept is particularly significant in areas like information visualization and VLSI design. The issue of determining whether a given graph can be drawn in an upward planar style has been explored since the 1960s, and in the 90s, researchers found that the problem can be reduced to a polynomial-time solvable issue by introducing specific constraints. However, in general cases, the problem is classified as NP-hard. This paper delves into the world of graph modification, proposing efficient algorithms to yield the smallest possible upward planar embedding for a given graph, along with a related problem of finding the smallest upward planar embedding when a specified number of vertices is added to a graph. These problems, referred to as Parameterized Constrained Upward Planarity (PCUP), are characterized by a single variable adjustment - either adding a specified number of vertices or edges - and a key constraint: maintaining a specified planar angle condition. The PCUP is an instance of a more complex problem, Bounded Face Constrained Upward Planarity (BFUP), which is itself a subset of a harder problem, Multi-Layered Upward Planarity (MUP). This paper presents a linear-time algorithm to convert an upward planar graph into an MUP, and subsequently, a parameterized logarithmic-time algorithm to convert an upward planar graph into an BFUP. These results are further utilized to yield efficient algorithms for PCUP: a parameterized efficient edge addition version (Parameterized Efficient Edge Addition, PEEA), a vertex addition version (Parameterized Efficient Vertex Addition, PEVA), and a multi-level version (Multi-Level Upward Planarity, MLUP). PEEA is the most efficient among the three, requiring a time of O((k + l)^{3/2} * n^2 log n), while PEVA requires a time of O(2^{(k+m)/4} * m^2 * n^2 log n), and MLUP requires a time of O((k+m)^{5/2} * n^2 log n). This research investigates the norm diminution principle for transfer operators, extending beyond the bounds of the hyperbolic dynamics framework. Specifically, we demonstrate the principle's applicability to semiflows in nonautonomous systems and conclude that under certain conditions, the total norm of the transfer operator family diminishes over time when the semiflow's hyperbolicity properties are established. Moreover, we show that for systems meeting certain analyticity criteria, the transfer operators' norms converge toward equilibrium at an exponential rate. These findings are illustrated through concrete applications involving analytic semiflows in both one-dimensional and infinite-dimensional settings, where we derive explicit dimension-dependent upper bounds for the rate of norm diminution. Ultimately, the principles derived in this research are expected to facilitate the development of dimension-dependent delay estimates for transfer operators, thereby contributing to a deeper understanding of transfer operators in nonautonomous systems. To support these claims, various numerical examples are presented, demonstrating the principle's efficacy in constructing analytic semiflows exhibiting dissipative and hyperbolic behavior. This research explores a broad class of multi-player contests known as non-local games, where players' payoffs are determined by both individual and joint efforts, regardless of players' relative positions. We identify a unique subgroup within non-local two-player contests where unique solutions exist, characterized by both individual and joint efforts being divisible by the smallest prime number. We prove that for contests within this subgroup, the minimum total effort required to achieve a given target payoff can be computationally determined. This finding reveals that such minimum total effort is not necessarily always divisible by the minimum prime number, as initially speculated. We further extend our analysis to multi-player contests, proving that for contests where players' efforts are independent, the minimum total effort required to achieve a given target profit is not only determinable but also computationally efficient to determine, especially in scenarios where the profit of individual players is considered separately. We present a replication pipeline, including crash input generation, symptom extraction, and guided reproduction. Our study replicates 8 out of 11 crashes from a diverse dataset with success rates of 80% and 100%, demonstrating the feasibility of GGP for crash replication.
