Object detection methods that can learn from unlabeled data have shown significant improvements. To achieve this, novel techniques like semi-supervised learning and pseudo-labeling have been explored. This paper introduces a unique pseudo-labeling strategy tailored to object detection, which involves generating image regions that guide downstream classification. These regions can be considered as initial bounding-box predictions, although they lack the necessary spatial information. To address this limitation, we propose a specialized lexicon object detector (LOD), a simplified object detection model designed to enhance pseudo-label accuracy by only using classification information. Our detector's design is motivated by open-world learning principles, which allow it to identify known objects and unknown entities. By integrating the lexicon object detector into our detection framework, we can significantly improve pseudo-label accuracy by first filtering out low-confidence predictions. Our experiments on two datasets demonstrate that this approach outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised methods by a substantial margin, with a 6.8% and 9.3% improvement in F1-score, respectively, on top of a strong supervised baseline. Our code is publicly available to facilitate future research. Additionally, we have conducted a series of ablation studies to provide insights into the lexicon object detector's design, as well as the pseudo-labeling strategy's robustness to lexicon size and transfer learning scenarios. Our findings suggest that a medium-sized lexicon (1,024 words) yields optimal results, although larger lexicons can potentially yield better outcomes. Moreover, we observe that transfer learning can be beneficial in certain scenarios, although the underlying patterns are more complex and dependent on the specific datasets in question. Ultimately, we believe that our research provides valuable lessons for the design of future unsupervised object detectors. Our research is the first to integrate open-world learning and transfer learning principles into the design of pseudo-labeling strategies for object detection, opening up new avenues of investigation. Our findings highlight the importance of spatial information in object detection and the potential benefits of leveraging unlabeled data with pseudo-labeling methods. However, the quality of pseudo-labels remains a critical limitation, and further research is required to address this challenge. Our research is an initial step towards improving pseudo-label quality, and we hope to stimulate the design of more sophisticated pseudo-labeling strategies that can effectively address the limitations of the current state-of-the-art methods. This paper seeks to address this limitation by developing an approach to divide the points into types and to apply it for the general case where the points interact with each other. The method employs a novel'stitching' technique, combining multiple Poisson point processes to create the desired pattern. The approach results in a straightforward and efficient algorithm for generating a Strauss model on any given area. The method's performance is demonstrated through a variety of examples, highlighting its practical applications. The study also shows that the Strauss model can be used as a foundation to develop other point process models. Finally, the research focuses on the limitations of the proposed algorithm and suggests potential future enhancements. In various real-world applications, multiple independent scheduling problems are concurrently processed for a limited number of time slots by multiple processors. Real-world scenarios include: (i) solving a collection of unrelated scheduling tasks simultaneously using Graphics Processing Units, (ii) distributing multiple hard real-time tasks onto Field-Programmable Gate Arrays, and (iii) dividing a set of flexible tasks across Central Processing Units to enhance their overall usage. We refer to this scheduling approach as the Multitasking Timetabling Problem (MTTP), characterized by: (a) a set of m identical processors, (b) n tasks with unique processing times, (c) a fixed number of K processors, (d) a limited time horizon T, and (d) each processor can only process at most K tasks at any given time. The objective is to determine a processing assignment of tasks to processors over time, minimizing the total completion time. We propose a polynomial-time algorithm, the Multitasking Timetabling Algorithm (MTTA), which iteratively constructs a feasible solution for the MTTP. Due to its computational simplicity and general applicability, MTTA serves as a baseline for future research. Furthermore, we evaluate the performance of MTTA through extensive numerical experiments conducted under various parameters and demonstrate its effectiveness in producing high-quality solutions. Additionally, we observe that MTTA-solved instances can be further improved by applying local search techniques. Consequently, we introduce an improved version of MTTA, referred to as MTTA+LS. Experimental results show that MTTA+LS produces high-quality solutions for a wide range of real-world applications. Moreover, MTTA+LS outperforms a benchmark solution generated by combining the best available single-processor algorithms in a straightforward manner. Consequently, MTTA+LS presents itself as a practical and efficient solution method for the MTTP. This study investigates how a single leg can jump on deformable ground, and vice versa. To tackle this complex issue, we break it down into two interconnected parts, analyzing the dynamics of a leg in different contexts. First, we model a leg as a hopper with an adjustable spring at the bottom, and use a simplified representation of the ground as a variable damping force. This simplification allows us to generate various leg motion patterns, which we apply to a control strategy to determine optimal spring stiffness, considering both energy storage and energy recovery. As a starting point for the second part, we simulate a leg attached to a body, modeled as a double mass system, and develop a feedback control strategy to enhance jumping performance, ultimately achieving a 25% increase in peak height relative to a traditional proportional-integral-derivative control method. Specifically, we investigated smooth, bounded domains in n-dimensional Euclidean space. Initially, we demonstrated well-posedness of smooth solutions for a Vlasov-Poisson-type system with a Newtonian interaction within confined domains. This involved proving the existence and uniqueness of smooth solutions up to a specific time interval. We then extended this finding to a related system modeling quartic interactions. This latter system is more challenging due to its non-local characteristics, which prevent direct application of standard techniques. To address this, we initially establish the existence of smooth solutions within a smaller domain and leverage a specific property related to quartic interactions to prove their continuation up to a specified time interval. This is an extension of existing research by Young, Stampacchia, and Giorgi. This study contributes to understanding the long-term behavior of smooth solutions for both systems. The emergence of these robust materials is primarily attributed to the formation of a percolating network of entangled strands. Ultrasonic energy, however, can disrupt these elastic connections and transform gels into liquids, allowing for gel reconstruction and liquid phase transition via vibration. When subjected to ultrasonic vibrations, both static and dynamic mechanical properties of these gels can be modified. In a study that explores this phenomenon, researchers utilized large particle-size distributions of polystyrene microspheres suspended in a styrene oil and exposed them to varying sonic conditions to assess changes in rheological behavior, particle distribution, and acoustic properties. The findings revealed that gel stiffness and viscosity can be reduced by strains similar to the elastic deformation of individual particles, while minimum shear strains are necessary to initiate gel destruction. Moreover, gel destruction strain is inversely related to the mean particle size, and sonic energy can either solidify or liquefy the gels depending on particle size. When subjected to cyclic loading, gel destruction occurs at lower strains than static forces, and lower shear moduli are observed in the extra-gel region. Microscopic analysis confirmed that ultrasonic vibrations disrupt and destroy individual connections between particles. In addition to altering gel properties, ultrasonic vibrations also modify the distribution of particles, resulting in the formation of particle aggregates. Acoustic properties of these gels, however, remain largely unaffected by gel destruction and the resulting liquid state. The study demonstrates that ultrasonic vibrations offer a unique means to manipulate and tailor the mechanical and flow properties of colloidal gels, paving the way for future applications in various processing and characterization techniques. Furthermore, the findings suggest that rheo-acoustic gels possess potential as smart materials in advanced technologies and devices. In a particular application, the method may facilitate the creation of ultrasonically-induced phase transitions in gels to support the growth of microorganisms, such as yeast, thereby enhancing bio-product yields. In summary, the research reveals that sonic energy can be utilized as an external stimulus to modify and control the properties of colloidal gels, ultimately transforming them into materials with tunable mechanical and flow characteristics. Secondly, these metrics focus solely on evaluation, neglecting the aspect of training summaries for high-quality samples. The proposed algorithm is adaptable to diverse observation models, has a time complexity of O(N^2), and is highly resilient to noise for a range of signal types, including functions, finite rational series, and neural networks' membrane potentials. While this issue is more complex than the initial reconstruction problem, we are able to leverage the rich mathematical structures associated with these problems, such as linear or quadratic programming, matrix analysis, or graph theory, to solve it efficiently. Hydrodynamic turbulence in liquids significantly differs from gas turbulence due to its higher viscosity, which influences its small-scale behavior. Understanding and modeling liquid turbulence accurately is essential for various natural and industrial processes, including ocean and atmospheric phenomena, where thermal effects play a crucial role. We present a new approach to modeling and numerical simulations of energy dissipation in homogeneous, anisotropic turbulent liquids, incorporating thermal properties and frictional heating. This approach utilizes a statistical model of turbulent energy based on the nearly incompressible Navier-Stokes equation and the Karhunen-Loeve basis. It also considers thermal disturbances and frictional heating in the context of molecular dynamics simulations of dissipation mechanisms. Our results from simulations match theoretical predictions of turbulent energy evolution and provide new insights into the nature of dissipation processes in thermally active liquids. Furthermore, we observe that the turbulent flow at the dissipation scale exhibits characteristics of infinite Prandtl number limits, which helps to explain some natural and industrial phenomena. For example, our results support the hypothesis that ocean and atmospheric turbulence result from processes similar to those occurring in the Earth's core. Additionally, our findings align with laboratory experiments of binary and multi-component melts under gravitational influence. They also shed light on the mechanisms of crystallization in melts and underpin the importance of frictional and thermal effects in processes like metal melting, dental and pad casting, and exoplanet core formation. Overall, our results confirm that thermal disturbances and frictional heating contribute to turbulent kinetic energy in high-Reynolds-number liquids, which in turn drives the turbulent flow at small scales. This work lays the groundwork for future studies on the behavior of turbulent liquids at the molecular level in various applications. It also opens up new avenues for research in the fields of liquid turbulence and thermal disturbance dynamics. This number quantifies the ratio of inertial to viscous forces in a system, and its magnitude can significantly impact the behavior of turbulent liquids. By analyzing the properties of velocity time series, researchers can gain valuable insights into the characteristics of turbulent liquids. The phenomenon of laser-induced gratings in liquids has garnered significant attention due to its production of complex and less common diffraction patterns such as Bragg, Lippesmann, and Talbot, as well as its potential to generate self-focusing and diffraction in liquids. Notably, it presents an alternative method for achieving self-phase modulation in liquids, bypassing the need for surface interaction. Research in the field has been limited, with most studies focusing on gas-phase diffraction patterns. To the best knowledge available, this paper initiates a comprehensive numerical analysis of the liquid-phase diffractive grating phenomena, including a detailed examination of the laser-induced self-focusing in liquids. The results of our study align with experimental observations by B. K. Tata in Curr. Sci., 2008. Our analysis revealed that the intensity of the diffracted light is directly proportional to the order of diffraction and that it decreases as the laser intensity increases. The observed patterns suggest that the laser-induced self-focusing in liquids is a consequence of the thermal effects induced by the incident laser light. The thermal profile is attributed to the absorption of laser energy by the liquid, with the absorbed energy being transferred to the surrounding liquid molecules through intermolecular forces. As a result of the thermal effects, the refractive index of the liquid near the incident region increases, leading to a deviation in the laser beam. The observed patterns such as the Bragg, Lippesmann, and Talbot, are a result of the interference between the incident and scattered laser beams. The numerical analysis presented in this paper enables a deeper understanding of the intricacies of the laser-induced diffractive grating phenomena in liquids. The study has significant implications for the generation of intense short-pulse lasers through liquid self-focusing. The numerical analysis can be employed to predict the laser-induced diffractive grating patterns in liquids for a given set of parameters including liquid properties, laser intensity, and wavelength. The study opens up new avenues for the manipulation and measurement of intense short-pulse lasers. The predicted patterns from our numerical analysis can be experimentally verified using techniques such as numerical aperture limitation, and they can be employed to predict the laser-induced diffractive grating patterns in gases for a given set of parameters including gas properties, laser intensity, and wavelength. The study has significant implications for the manipulation and measurement of intense short-pulse lasers. The numerical model employed in this paper can be used to predict the laser-induced diffractive grating patterns in liquids and gases.

A method is developed to calculate the higher-order corrections in the standard model expansion for processes involving the production of top and bottom quarks via gluon fusion. This method incorporates the complete set of self-energy corrections for all quarks, including extended top and bottom quark graphs that are not typically considered in the effective theory approach. We specifically examine the sensitivity of numerical results to the mass of quarks beyond the standard model expansion. An updated code is also introduced to facilitate this calculation, allowing for the direct determination of top and bottom quark production cross-sections without the need for a effective theory description. We anticipate this code will be beneficial in the study of top quark physics at future colliders, such as the HL-LHC and FCC-hh. An example of its application demonstrates its potential to provide insights into the mass of quarks beyond the standard model expansion with high precision, with a mass resolution of approximately 20 MeV and 10 MeV for top and bottom quarks, respectively. We particularly emphasize the importance of including these higher-order corrections in the study of bottom quark physics at the LHC, given its relatively high sensitivity to the mass of quarks beyond the standard model expansion. In the study of top quark physics, these higher-order corrections are found to have a relatively minor impact, with a mass uncertainty of less than 1 MeV. We also highlight the potential of these higher-order corrections to be further reduced through the use of top quark tagging techniques. Furthermore, an alternative method of calculation is developed, which does not rely on the use of graphs that are not typically considered in the standard model expansion. This work presents the first systematic analysis of pre-trained language models' zero-shot learning performance across multiple cue collections, revealing significant variations in their ability to generalize. Our model's exceptional performance on cue collections that were not seen during training highlights its superior adaptability. Recommender systems face significant challenges in justifying their recommendations and addressing user concerns. To address this issue, it is crucial for models to grasp the underlying motivations of users, which helps in generating transparent and understandable suggestions. Unfortunately, users' intrinsic motivations are difficult to determine due to their subjective nature and varied complexities. This research introduces a new technique for modeling a user's hidden motivation, which is assumed to correspond to a class label, by extracting valuable insights from their sequential behavior over time. A multi-instance learning framework is employed, which involves training an inner classifier to predict the user's motivation class by utilizing local representations of instances that are learned using an inner model. This innovative approach enables the inner model to capture intricate patterns in user behavior and map them to specific motivation classes. A theoretical analysis demonstrates the relationship between the inner and inner classifiers, which shows that the inner model's ability to generalize improves as the user's motivation classes become more distinct. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art benchmark algorithms in terms of their performance on text-free and text-enhanced recommendation tasks. Moreover, the research demonstrates that the inner model can generate understandable and complex user behavior patterns at a sentence level, which outperforms existing sequential recommender models. Finally, the research involves an in-depth analysis of the inner model's outputs through an eye-tracking study, which reveals that the user's motivation class corresponds to a specific semantic concept, which can be accurately identified by the inner model. This research provides novel insights into the inner workings of a user's mind, which can be utilized to develop more effective and transparent recommender systems. A user study has confirmed that the inner model's outputs align with human expectations. Interestingly, the research has found that the inner model's bias towards specific motivation classes can be manipulated by adjusting its hyperparameters, which may have significant implications for the entire system. This research has shed light on the importance of understanding the hidden user motivation for developing more accurate and transparent recommender systems. The integration of Artificial Intelligence techniques and Vehicle-to-Everything technologies has significantly improved the quality of life and transportation comfort. However, large amounts of data are required to train advanced AI models, which presents a challenge due to the limitations of individual vehicles. Federated Learning has the potential to address this issue by enabling vehicles to utilize their neighboring peers' data while maintaining the confidentiality of their local information. Although traditional Blockchain technologies can be applied to Federated Learning, there is a lack of comprehensive frameworks that accommodate both. In this study, a thorough analysis of Blockchain supported Federated Learning frameworks for Internet of Vehicles is conducted, focusing on their underlying components, security features, and scalability measures. In addition, a comparison based on various evaluation metrics is performed, and it is observed that there is a knowledge gap regarding the selection of suitable Blockchain technologies and Federated Learning algorithms. In order to fill this gap, a novel Blockchain supported Federated Learning framework is proposed, incorporating a Distributed Ledger Technology, a Secure Communication protocol, and an Advanced Encryption method to ensure data privacy and integrity. This proposed framework is evaluated using a comprehensive set of simulation-based metrics, and it is found to be superior to existing solutions in terms of performance. In particular, it is noted that Blockchain technologies can be optimized to reduce processing overhead, while the adoption of Federated Learning algorithms can be fine-tuned to improve accuracy and convergence speed. Ultimately, this proposed framework is found to be a practical solution, and it is recommended for adoption in real-world applications. Future research directions are also identified, and they are expected to further enhance the performance of Blockchain supported Federated Learning frameworks for Internet of Vehicles in the future. These research directions include the development of in-network computing and edge caching techniques, the exploration of new Blockchain technologies and Federated Learning algorithms, and the potential integration of other emerging technologies, such as Software-defined Networking and Multi-agent systems. In summary, this paper provides an in-depth review of Blockchain supported Federated Learning frameworks for Internet of Vehicles, and it is found that there is a need to develop more advanced and flexible frameworks that can be tailored to the unique requirements of vehicles. This paper also serves as a knowledge base for researchers and practitioners working in this field, and it is expected to inspire future research directions and innovations in the development of Internet of Vehicles systems. This research investigates and compares the performance of several machine learning algorithms for predicting non-pliable lobe disease given known lung CT scans and patient data. We employed eight distinct algorithms, assessed their accuracy using multiple evaluation methods, and analyzed the features with the highest predictive value. Our findings demonstrate that the random forest algorithm yielded the highest overall accuracy score of 85%, followed by the support vector machine with an accuracy score of 80%. The gradient boosting algorithm recorded the highest F1 score of 83%, alongside the support vector machine with an accuracy score of 80%. Consistently, the support vector machine emerged as the top performer across all accuracy metrics. Our analysis identified distinct sets of critical features for different algorithms, suggesting varying combinations influence an algorithm's accuracy depending on its type. This work aims to lay the groundwork for future research in this area. We plan to expand our model to predict multiple related diseases, including non-pliable lobe disease, using an ensemble of machine learning algorithms, and explore the feasibility of semi-supervised disease prediction. Moreover, our feature importance analysis will be used to identify the most relevant CT scan properties that contribute to disease prediction. These results will be used to develop a decision support tool for predicting the presence or absence of a specific lobe disease based on patient data and CT scan information. We also intend to apply transfer learning to utilize pre-trained models on related tasks and then adapt them to predict non-pliable lobe disease. Finally, our future research will involve the integration of feature selection methods to reduce the impact of noisy data and improve model interpretability. We will achieve this by only utilizing the most relevant features that maximize the classification difference between different disease classes. Consequently, our model will be characterized by improved accuracy, higher generalizability, and lower complexity. complicated, especially when dealing with energy-constrained devices such as
smartphones and sensor nodes. A power-efficient design is crucial for the
practical deployment of such systems. A strategy to improve power efficiency is
to use local data, which generally requires less power to access than remote
sources. However, the effectiveness of this approach has not been thoroughly
investigated in the context of machine learning. This study aims to bridge this
gap and examines when utilizing local data is beneficial for boosting the
resilience of machine learning systems. We evaluate the advantages of incorporating
local labels, noisy labels, and partial data in boosting image classification
models, which face significant challenges due to their large memory requirements. 
Our findings demonstrate that leveraging local data can be very beneficial when
there are substantial differences between remote and local distributions. However, 
using local data may not always be advantageous when there are significant shifts 
in data distribution. We also show that accessing complete local datasets can be
helpful in certain scenarios, which is particularly significant given the limited
storage capacity for large images. Overall, our study highlights the need for
further research into the design of machine learning systems that are resilient to

This version bypasses expensive matrix inverses by utilizing a sequence of easily inverting matrices. This paper further develops that work by precisely characterizing the class of matrices that can be easily inverted. We also derive a closed-form expression for the optimal transport problem's solution that applies when the Sinkhorn weights are collinear. This achievement allows us to reduce the computational complexity of the most resource-intensive loop in the Sinkhorn algorithm from quadratic to linear while retaining precise error guarantees. This improved implementation, which we refer to as CTSinkhorn, demonstrates superior performance on real-world datasets by outperforming both the standard Sinkhorn algorithm and the QSinkhorn variant, especially in scenarios with moderate to high scaling parameters. We aim to develop a novel view generation technique that captures and maintains the essence of a scene from a single perspective, resulting in an endless variety of viewpoints. Traditional generative models excel in creating diverse views but often sacrifice consistency. In contrast, generative adversarial networks struggle to scale due to high computation costs. To overcome these limitations, we introduce the DiffDreamer, an effective solution leveraging a conditional diffusion model, which generates high-quality, endlessly diverse views at a significantly lower computational cost. The model's training relies on synthetic data created by combining two perspectives, one of which is known and the other unknown, allowing it to learn the scene's characteristics independently of the view angle. As a result, even when given just a single view, the DiffDreamer can generate realistic and varied synthetic views. Through extensive testing on various datasets, we demonstrate the superiority of the DiffDreamer over existing techniques in producing realistic and diverse views. Notably, our model outperforms state-of-the-art methods in creating realistic single-view synthetic data, as validated by a human evaluation of 15 popular datasets. Complex systems' control and prediction have historically relied on modeling approaches that either utilize system identification or assume knowledge of the underlying dynamics. In this study, a novel framework is introduced, enabling prediction, improvement, and control of complex networks solely through the analysis of interconnected data. The framework is initially tested on a model simulating the spread of a highly contagious disease (epidemic model) through networks comprised of interacting units. The model's parameters were determined by a non-parametric approach, and a data-driven strategy was developed to identify and mitigate disease outbreaks. The outcomes show that the early implementation of the control method can prevent massive epidemics and that the use of the framework on a limited dataset is feasible even in large networks. The findings suggest that the control costs are inversely related to the network's structural properties. Our research focuses on developing a hate speech detection model through the incorporation of a novel characteristic extraction module. The dataset used for training and testing purposes comprises 12,514 annotated samples derived from 7,295 online posts. Our proposed architecture, consisting of two recurrent neural network-based layers and a characteristic extraction module, has yielded impressive results, surpassing state-of-the-art models in their context variables. Specifically, our model's predictive accuracy amounts to 81.8% for four-fold cross-validation evaluations. This achievement not only underscores the model's efficacy but also highlights the value of the proposed characteristic extraction module as a standalone component in other machine learning models. Our study's implications suggest that the integration of such a module can enhance the model's capacity to mitigate errors stemming from the encoding of biases. Ultimately, our model's success serves as a strong foundation for the moderation of social media content and the preservation of online social harmony. In the realm of computer vision, particularly with MatchNet-based metric learning, a MatchNet consists of a key encoder, a query encoder, and a matcher, working in tandem to calculate query-batch similarities. A common architecture for the encoders is a siamese structure, with Mutual Information Maximization (MIM) performed between the query and batch features. However, this siamese setup can be inefficient due to its separate feature extractors. To address this limitation, papers such as this one aim to improve the encoders by merging their features into a single Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) structure. A MIMO consists of a shared encoder, with two separate branches - a key and a query - that use the shared features to calculate query-batch similarities. While this MIMO structure has shown promise, the separate feature dimensionality can make training more complicated. To resolve this, this paper proposes two training methods: a straightforward approach that utilizes a linear coupling layer, and an alternative method that employs a nonlinear Bottleneck layer. The experiments indicate that both training methods are effective and lead to improved training and accuracy when implemented in MatchNet. Moreover, the proposed MIMO-MatchNet approach outperforms the existing MatchNet baseline, achieving up to a 2.0% higher mean Average Precision on the CUB dataset. To enhance the precision and consistency of industrial robots, a proposed method utilizes supplementary position sensors on the actuator's shafts in conjunction with the existing external measurement systems, like vision systems, for real-time trajectory correction. When a commanded input is fed into the robot's control system, the additional sensors measure the actuator's rotational position accuracy, and the algorithm calculates the optimal adjustment to compensate for the detected discrepancies, sending an updated trajectory to the robot for execution. This method demonstrates a notable improvement in following the desired path, especially at increased frequencies and for complex motions. Evaluations were performed on an actual six-degree-of-freedom KUKA LBR iiwa, and the results indicate that, when auxiliary sensors are involved, the root mean square error in the position vector can decrease by more than 60% in some cases, and the maximum error is reduced by at least 40%. Moreover, the presence of auxiliary sensors enables a significant increase in the robot's bandwidth, resulting in a greater than 50% increase in the highest frequency of position data, and smoother overall motion. When the external position measurement system is unavailable, the proposed strategy relies solely on the auxiliary sensors to generate the optimal control input for the actuator, and the algorithm's stability is proven using the Lyapunov inequality. This method was successfully tested in scenarios with and without external position measurement, and the calculated control parameters exhibit smooth and continuous behavior, as desired. A critical parameter in the algorithm determines the extent of adjustment based on the detected error, and when this value is set to zero, the original uncomplicated control strategy is restored. The proposed method was also evaluated using a detailed model of the six-degree-of-freedom flexible beam to verify its effectiveness, and the results indicate that it can significantly enhance the robot's performance, even when model inaccuracies are considered, by accurately capturing the discrepancies between simulated and actual motion, and the observed benefits are shown to be consistent with the theoretical predictions. This method is adaptable to various types of feedback, actuator dynamics, and constraints, and can be applied to control systems with similar characteristics, even when the dynamics are nonlinear, as long as the actuator's rotational position accuracy can be measured in real-time. A potential limitation of the proposed strategy is the necessity for external validation to ensure the presence and accuracy of the detected position errors, and a more detailed discussion of this requirement is provided in the paper's supplementary material. This research investigates a new statistical approach called Multiple State Examination (MoSE), which analyzes complex, multi-faceted data from various fields such as health sciences and education. We utilize a data set that follows patients who experienced a myocardial infarction and focuses on their long-term health trajectories over nearly a decade. Our objective is to identify individuals who are at a higher risk of suffering from additional cardiovascular diseases or other health issues that require hospitalization, and to determine which factors contribute to these risks. By applying MoSE to this data, we can better understand the interrelated health problems that arise after a myocardial infarction and how they are affected by age, social background, physical health at the beginning of the study, and changes in physical and mental well-being over time. MoSE enables us to model the complex, interconnected patterns of health issues among this demographic and how they are influenced by life-style factors, as well as to assess the effectiveness of interventions aimed at preventing or mitigating these risks. Furthermore, our model accounts for the limitations of the data collection, which includes missing or incomplete information, as well as the potential biases resulting from the data's dual nature (i.e., from the perspective of the individual or the healthcare system). Our application of MoSE involves a model selection process that is based on theoretical principles rather than a purely frequency-based approach, which is often inconsistent and may not provide valid results in all cases. Ultimately, our model highlights the importance of examining the multiple dimensions of health and social issues, which are often highly correlated with one another, in order to better understand the underlying health dynamics and how they can be improved. By adopting a more holistic perspective, we can gain a deeper understanding of the specific factors that contribute to an individual's risk of experiencing additional health issues or, in the case of our study, suffering from a second myocardial infarction. To address the challenge of efficiently simulating long-time molecular dynamics, we develop the molecular continuum (MC). The MC represents the complex electronic structure of a molecule as a solution to a nonlinear partial differential equation (PDE) that converges to a equilibrium state. By approximating this PDE with a linear one through a quadrature approach based on the thermodynamic integration of path-integral concepts, we arrive at a set of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) that facilitate the analysis of their numerical properties. A thorough investigation of the stability and convergence properties of the ODEs enables the simulation of multiple-site models, including those applicable to peptides and proteins. Furthermore, MC simulations can be optimized using an adjoint-based approach to refine parameters such as non-bonded interactions, resulting in strong agreement between our four-site model and high-fidelity quantum dynamics simulations in the ground state. Additionally, our three-site model is shown to effectively capture non-equilibrium molecular processes, including the desorption of a molecule from a surface. Ultimately, our findings indicate that MC offers a promising compromise between computational simplicity and modeling accuracy. With further advancements, MC may become a valuable tool in accelerating quantum-based molecular dynamics simulations. A crucial dimension in medical image categorization is image labeling. Unfortunately, due to the time-consuming and skill-intensive process involved, real labeling images are often in short supply, while the existing labels often prove ineffective. As a result, deep learning models often perform subpar when encountering noisy or mislabeled data. To counter this issue, our research introduces the Bayesian Statistics Directed Label Renovation (BSDLR) method. Unlike previous techniques that utilize unsupervised learning to correct labels, our approach relies on data with partial correct labels, ensuring that the corrected dataset remains consistent with the original. By employing a Label Confidence Score (LCS) to determine the likelihood and reliability of existing labels, BSDLR uses this information to identify and correct the errors made during the training process. At the image level, a Local Spatial Distance (LSD) metric measures the local spatial consistency, while Bayesian statistics ensure that the global corrected label distribution aligns with the original dataset. Experimental results show that BSDLR achieves an accuracy of 85.11% on the noisy Datasets G1, G2, G3, and G4, surpassing state-of-the-art models by 8-15% and demonstrating robust generalizability. Moreover, BSDLR corrects labels more effectively than existing methods, with the distribution of corrected labels showing improved consistency. Ultimately, BSDLR outperforms other noise mitigation techniques in medical image categorization. The source code for BSDLR is available on GitHub at https://github.com/whu-mlsl/BSDLR.git. With this model, real-world datasets can be trained and tested using the online demo at http://www.whu-mlsl.com/BSDLR. Our model has been successfully applied to the classification of lung nodules, achieving state-of-the-art results. An accompanying video is available at https://youtu.be/1gkq4xuKX9g. This research paper examines the electronic properties of a unique system
composed of silicene, surrounded by hexagonal boron nitride and doped with
manganese. Utilizing density functional theory, we find that manganese substitutes
into the sublattice of Pmna-structure silicene, and that the surrounding
hexagonal boron nitride results in a negligible charge transfer between the two
layers. Contrary to our expectations, the manganese atom exhibits a +2
oxidation state, and its 3d electrons show a tendency to form anti-bonding
orbitals within the two-dimensional silicene layer. Furthermore, our analysis
reveals that the manganese atom's interaction with surrounding electrons is
significantly altered due to the presence of environment-induced spin-orbit
effects, making it a potential candidate for the creation of a topologically unique
state known as quantum spin Hall effect. This unique arrangement of manganese
doped silicene is found to be stable under both uniaxial and isotropic strain, and
can be easily produced using chemical vapour deposition and subsequent annealing. 
The findings of our study hold significant potential for the development of
innovative, stable, and efficient spintronics and quantum computing devices.

Our results revealed that a linear combination of oversampling methods correlated with better performance, and the choice of linear combination depended on the specific problem being addressed. We observed improved performance over single method oversampling, and better performance compared to a baseline system in 93% of trials, with notable improvement for the three datasets we used (0208, Markov, and WebKB-SG), particularly in out-of-vocabulary scenarios where oversampling was beneficial. Our findings suggest that linearly combining oversampling methods addresses the limitations of individual techniques and offers a more robust solution for data imbalance problems. Additionally, our results demonstrate the potential for improved out-of-vocabulary handling through oversampling in a text categorization context. Overall, our work highlights the importance of considering multiple artificial oversampling methods and combining them to address data class imbalance issues effectively. The inherent unpredictability of adversarial noise may hinder model performance and explainability. To counteract this, researchers often rely on overly conservative models that prioritize accuracy over exploration. This study proposes an adaptive approach, employing data amplification techniques to balance the trade-off between model accuracy and explainability. A novel amplification method using transfer learning is presented, along with its theoretical underpinnings using statistical learning theory. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that in high noise regimes, data amplification facilitates statistical learning, while also revealing an optimal balance between model complexity and loss adjustment. Lastly, the results of synthetic and real-world experiments validate the effectiveness of data amplification in boosting model performance and generalization. Notably, the method shows remarkable resilience to catastrophic gradients in linear models and achieves state-of-the-art performance in adversarial fingerprinting tasks. Source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/andreabelli/data-amplification.

A solid-state spin laser utilizes electronic spins as the primary excitation mechanism instead of vibrational phonons. Although more efficient in certain materials, electronic excitation faces challenges in lasing due to restricted spin flip rates. To overcome this limitation, researchers have proposed the concept of a electronic alkali spin laser. By incorporating alkali metals with strong spin flip rates into a ring resonator combined with high-quality optical fibers, scientists have developed a potential laser technology that could operate at near-infrared wavelengths. This innovative laser design capitalizes on the unique properties of certain rare earth ions actuated by the alkali metals to provide coherent optical signals. A proposed configuration features doped fibers connected to a alkali metal fiber laser, paired with a rare earth ion waveguide laser, allowing for potential application in mid-infrared generation through the principle of difference frequency generation. A functioning prototype has demonstrated the feasibility of generating narrow linewidth signals within the range of 600-800 nanometers and has shown potential for further development into a high-performance optical coherent transceiver for data transfer across long distances. The mid-infrared generation capability could also serve as a model for generating coherent light within this spectral range, offering various applications across biomedical and environmental fields. A significant advantage of this technology is the ability to safely handle toxic materials within a closed system, thus minimizing potential risks. This article outlines the underlying principles of this emerging technology and presents a prototype that demonstrates significant progress towards the realization of an electronic alkali spin laser. A notable aspect of this research is the ability to maintain long-term stability in the device, a crucial factor for applications in optical coherent data transfer. The development of this technology could potentially lead to the creation of a laser that operates at room temperature with long-term chemical and biological compatibility. A future direction for this research could involve further investigation into the properties of certain materials as potential alkali metal sources, including cesium and rubidium, to identify the most suitable option. A future demonstration of this technology could involve generating coherent mid-infrared light through the application of a non-linear crystal in a laboratory setting, offering a significant step towards the practical implementation of this innovative laser design. Furthermore, the connection between JT gravity and this particle model can be extended to the worldsheet theory level, showing that JT gravity's thermal state is also represented by a time-dependent version of the Liouville theory's radial Hamiltonian. This connection enables us to calculate the expectation value of Liouville CFT's stress tensor within the c=−24 universal conformal block's thermal state, thereby resolving an open question from the 1990s regarding the stress tensor's expectation value in the Liouville theory's ground state. The calculations reveal that these expectations exhibit time-dependent oscillations and linear time dependencies, respectively. Using the established correspondence, we are able to interpret these results as originating from the properties of non-interacting fermions within the context of the "massive Q-lab" particle model. Lastly, we explore the implications of the obtained results in relation to the black hole and tunneling physics as well as to the properties of one-dimensional disordered systems. Human brains are wired to learn from past experiences, utilizing various techniques, such as trial and error, to acquire new skills. Although parietal cortex plays a key role in this learning process, the underlying methods employed by individuals can significantly vary. To explore this individual difference in learning, we conducted a study where healthy adults participated in a probabilistic eye movement task, which allowed us to monitor their brains in response to prediction errors, assess their skill acquisition, and evaluate the effectiveness of their strategies. Our results show that participants who developed more efficient methods tended to exhibit greater activity in response to negative prediction errors, and also demonstrated better performance and faster learning. These findings suggest that midbrain structures play a significant role in identifying suboptimal actions, and that an individual's likelihood of using effective learning strategies is influenced by their brain's ability to detect errors, which ultimately determines their overall skill acquisition. These results have important implications for the development of more effective learning and cognitive training interventions. Furthermore, we found that effective learning strategies are characterized by a consistent pattern of action-reaction sequences over time, and that this consistency is closely tied to the activity of midbrain structures that recognize prediction errors. In contrast, less efficient learners exhibited more variable and sometimes contradictory sequences. These results suggest that part of the explanation for individual differences in learning lies in the underlying organizational patterns of their learning strategies, which can either be consistent or variable. These findings are significant because they reveal that individual differences in learning are not only a matter of skill acquisition but also of the underlying organizational structures of those skills. These results have important implications for the development of more effective learning and cognitive training interventions. The Frechet distance, however, allows for efficient soft approximations both in continuous and discrete space. Although soft Frechet is more suitable for time series, it still has limitations, particularly for short sequences. This paper addresses a time series approximation problem using the Frechet distance, showing that certain limits cannot be exceeded for exact nearest neighbor search, and proposing an algorithm with estimated bounds for approximate search. This paper presents a new variational framework for reconstructing and analyzing images taken from CT scans with multiple energy settings, using data from a linear system affected by noise. By breaking down the reconstruction process into two steps, we first apply an image reconstruction step that uses a linear method, and then a second step for analyzing the reconstructed images, using a non-linear technique. A comprehensive investigation of a single Mn atom and Mn dimers attached to a niobium surface using scanning tunneling microscopy has led to the observation of various Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states. Analyzing these states employs a theoretical model grounded in initial principles, which generates an effective Hamiltonian in momentum space. Subsequent many-body calculations are performed utilizing a relativistic version of the Numana--Shiba--Rusinov model. Formulated as an relativistic initial principles theory, this model is compatible with density functional theory and enables the computation of Green's functions and local density of states. By comparing the results to experimental findings, it was found that an alignment of the magnetization with the crystallographic axis is favored over alignment with the surface normal. Furthermore, numerical calculations of the local density of states and magnetization were conducted and compared to numerical many-body results and experimental data obtained from spin-polarized low-energy electron microscopy. All results demonstrate the effectiveness of the theoretical model in describing the complex behavior of magnetic impurities in a superconducting host material. A method for comparing two elements of a partially ordered set is considered. 
For any pair of the set elements $a$ and $b$, if there exist an element $x$ and a sequence of the set's elements $a \leq x_1, \ldots, x_n = b$ such that each element in the sequence is either $a$ or $b$, we say $a$ is related to $b$ via $x$. 
If such a sequence exists for both $a \leq b$ and $b \leq a$, we say $a$ and $b$ are dual comparables with respect to the set, denoted as $a \mathrel{\text{dual-comp}} b$.

This new attention mechanism sheds light on DCNN's semantic adaptation capabilities, providing novel insights into DCNN's hidden layer structures and the underlying principles of representation learning. This approach holds significant potential for the development of next-generation neural networks with enhanced transparency. A cutting-edge approach to preserve crucial visual details in obfuscation techniques is the reversible concealment. In this field, our contribution is an innovative method of restoring the exact original image from a combined format containing an object superimposed onto a background. This technique has practical implications for various applications such as data protection, security, and even forensic analysis. Presently, available methods rely on iterative processes that require precise settings and often result in partial distortion of the original image. Our solution, an advanced neural network model, can generate high-quality inverse transformations with minimal visual distortions automatically. The model is trained using a combination of generative adversarial networks, which enables the creation of a precise one-to-one correspondence between the transformed and original images. The model's training data is generated using a novel approach that employs a series of iterative processes with progressively larger patches to simulate real-world scenarios. The model's effectiveness is evaluated through comprehensive testing, which includes multiple metrics, and experimental results demonstrate its superiority over existing solutions in terms of visual quality and accuracy. To our knowledge, this study marks the first attempt at applying advanced neural networks to the field of reversible concealment. The model's implementation is publicly available and can be easily adapted to other related applications. Moreover, our research highlights the benefits of employing neural networks to overcome the limitations of existing iterative methods, leading to a significant improvement in quality and accuracy. The model's performance is characterized by a high correlation value of 0.9995 and Mean Squared Error (MSE) of 2.35e-5 between the restored and original images, as evidenced by the results of our testing protocol. The model's accuracy is further reinforced by its ability to consistently produce high-quality results, with 93% of images scoring above 0.9 on the SSIM scale. To our surprise, the model's complexity is relatively modest, with a Fr\'echet Inception Distance score of 4.88 and parameter count of 580K, enabling it to be applied in real-world settings. Ultimately, our solution's potential applications extend beyond reversible concealment to various other fields. By applying a conservative finite element method, our model extends the diffusion equation to solve a nonlinear problem with linear growth rates and qualitatively accurate solutions. This model can be applied to study how density and flow evolve over time, enabling the use of an anisotropic diffusion coefficient to study mass transport. Notably, our model maintains consistency even when initial conditions become negative, extending its potential uses to a broader range of problems. Finally, we apply our model to a study of how quasilinear diffusion affects the formation of structures in kinetic theory. This model has the potential to improve our understanding of plasma dynamics and turbulence by enabling the use of local theories to solve complex, nonlinear problems. This paper investigates the divergence properties of two families of groups related to Thompson's groups, specifically $\mathcal G_n$, $n\ge 2$, and braided Thompson groups $Br_n$, $n\ge 3$. It's observed that only $G_2$ exhibits finite divergence; all other groups have infinite divergence. Furthermore, our results show that the braided Thompson groups share the same finite or infinite divergence properties as their respective subgroups $G_{n-1}$. Notably, this research settles the first part of Open Problem 3.12 in the 2019 book 'New perspectives in probability and statistics', asking whether every subgroup of a group with finite divergence also has finite divergence. It's now known that this is not the case, as exemplified by the subgroup $\langle br_{n-1}, br_n \rangle$ in $Br_n$ for $n \ge 3$. With this goal in mind, we've developed a method for building directed networks that integrate two key attachment processes. The first involves a preference-based system where existing nodes with more connections attract new nodes, while the second promotes a more random distribution of connections. By combining these mechanisms, our approach allows for a high degree of customization, enabling researchers to generate networks with a wide range of density, diameter, and strong and weak cycle counts. We've demonstrated the efficacy of our method using a well-known preferential attachment model as a starting point and applied it to a range of exemplary scenarios, including social influence and information diffusion. The resulting networks, produced by our directionless growth process, exhibit a range of target properties without the need for manual network pruning. Furthermore, our approach can also generate networks with a core-periphery structure, where a large central core is surrounded by peripheral nodes. The output from our process typically requires minimal post-processing adjustments, making it a highly efficient and effective tool for network creation. Notably, the resulting statistics from our method align closely with the actual statistics of the produced networks, providing a high level of transparency and understanding of the underlying attachment dynamics. This paper introduces a new method for creating Gaussian Process kernels based on underlying mathematical equations. It is often challenging for Gaussian Process models to learn complex interactions between data points due to their black-box nature. In contrast, our approach provides explicit mathematical expressions that can be used to understand and analyze the learned connections. By adapting established mathematical formulas related to random variables, we developed a set of flexible Gaussian Process kernels that can handle various input and output scenarios. Our kernels can easily accommodate multi-dimensional inputs and outputs, and are also compatible with categorical data. The presence of problematic or confusing code smells within software test cases can
negatively impact developers' productivity and collaboration. While prior research has
investigated programmers' perceptions towards code smells in general, it is unclear how
test code smells are viewed by practitioners. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted
a study that gathered over 200 developer responses. Our findings indicate that a wide
range of programmers is affected by test code smells, with many developers expressing
frustration and annoyance. We also discovered that programmers tend to be more critical
of their peers for not addressing test code smells compared to code smells in main code
files. Our research provides a foundation for investigating the impact of social cues on the
propagation of technical debt in software development. Furthermore, we hope that by
highlighting developers' collective views on the significance of test code smells, our work
can motivate developers to give priority to eliminating test code smells when addressing
technical debt. The research data, including code and survey responses, are publicly
available and can be accessed via https://github.com/ahmadnia/test_smells_developer_viewpoint.

smells, which is a novel finding. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to

The spectator has limited information, knowing only the state of the actor and the reward function, but cannot directly observe either. To overcome this, the spectator must infer the actor's policy by utilizing available information. Our research delves into how well this can be achieved, with a focus on the ease of computation and a relevant theoretical framework. Additionally, we examine the creation of spectatorial policies that are grounded in human decision-making principles, such as exploration of the environment. Finally, we assess the challenges involved in directly training a spectator policy, as well as the effectiveness of a new method that combines supervised learning with reinforcement learning. This method, reverse reinforcement learning, offers an alternative to traditional reinforcement learning, allowing us to derive a parametric model of optimal spectator behavior without requiring the actor to interact with the environment. Our approach demonstrates that well-defined reward functions and sufficient data from the actor's policy are sufficient for the extraction of optimal spectator behaviors. Moreover, we demonstrate that these optimal spectator behaviors can be used to improve the actor's policy through policy opposition, resulting in policies that are more sample-efficient and robust. Our research findings are relevant to both machine learning and the philosophical study of reverse agency, with implications for understanding reverse causality and agency. Our work marks a significant step towards the extraction of high-level explanations of agent behavior from observed data, a long-standing goal in machine learning and reverse engineering. Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are gaining popularity for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) due to their potential in modeling complex systems with high dimensionality and incomplete physics. However, they have limitations in practical applications, primarily due to the high risk of overfitting, which necessitates more emphasis on uncertainty quantification. In this work, a straightforward approach is proposed to quantify the uncertainty of PINNs by incorporating data from actual experiments. A statistical analysis of the residuals between observed data and PINN predictions enables the estimation of posterior uncertainties. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance on both numerical and real-world examples compared to existing deep learning techniques and theoretical physics-based models. One notable success is the authentication of experimental results for the case of laser-induced forward scattering (LIFS) chemical detection. The proposed method not only validates the PINN results but also indicates that the recorded experimental data of PINN residuals show no anomalies, thus confirming the validity of the recorded data. In contrast, the presence of anomalous data can be easily identified by the proposed method, which highlights the importance of normalization in the presence of noise. The ability of the proposed method to authenticate both data and models makes it a reliable tool for validation, and it has significant implications for the deployment of machine learning models in real-world applications. Moreover, the proposed method can be used as a data diagnostic tool to aid in the interpretation of experimental results. A major challenge in developing more resilient models lies in the adaptive nature of GNNs, which requires exploring various network architectures during training. This work proposes a reinforcement learning framework for automatically selecting GNN modules and graph filtering algorithms on a task-specific basis, thereby enhancing model robustness and transferring to unrelated datasets. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in dealing with data contamination in image analysis applications involving graph data. A GitHub repository containing the project's source code has been made publicly available for further development.

The process of matching between star catalogs and various sky surveys has been improved by incorporating photometric data from multiple layers, in addition to traditional astrometry. In traditional astrometric matching, a given catalog is cross-referenced with survey images based on their celestial location, but this method is susceptible to errors in some catalogs and surveys. By incorporating photometric data, which is less prone to similar errors, we can increase the accuracy of matches. A novel algorithm called PhotMatch has been developed to leverage this additional information. It uses a Monte Carlo framework to calculate the probability of matches between potential catalog-sources and applies Bayesian statistics to incorporate the probability distribution. PhotMatch's performance is demonstrated on a set of artificial surveys and real data from the Gaia DR2 and Pan-STRRR, achieving higher accuracy and precision compared to traditional astrometric matching. Furthermore, we utilize the method to re-analyze the data from Gaia DR2 and Pan-STRRR, identifying 2 million sources that were missed in the original cross-referencing process, with an average offset of less than 0.1 arcseconds. The updated source list is available for download at https://www.astro-wise.org/. Additionally, the PhotMatch tool is open-sourced and can be accessed directly at https://github.com/panstarrssurveys/photmatch. A cloud-based web platform has also been developed at https://photmatch.cloud, enabling users to perform cross-referencing between any available sky surveys and catalogs. A free API is also available for developers to utilize. In the future, we plan to integrate the PhotMatch algorithm into the Gaia Data Release Process and expand the scope of the tool to support cross-referencing with any additional photometric data sources. Ontologies provide a structured way of representing knowledge, with concepts and relationships helping to organize complex information spaces. Visual representations are essential for understanding these intricate structures, but many current tools focus on hierarchical relationships, neglecting the importance of non-hierarchical connections. To address this imbalance, we introduce OntoPlot, a novel interactive visualization tool that seamlessly integrates node-link and space visualization principles to showcase both hierarchical and non-hierarchical relationships within large ontologies. By incorporating innovative features such as guided navigation and focal zooming, as well as the ability to adjust visualization complexity and filter out less relevant information, OntoPlot enables users to efficiently explore complex ontologies characterized by a mix of dense and sparse structures. To evaluate its effectiveness, we conducted a usability study comparing OntoPlot to existing tools, highlighting its benefits in exploring non-hierarchical connections as a single entity or individual relationships. The results demonstrate OntoPlot's potential to enhance performance in ontology-based data access, semantic search, and related fields. We introduce an innovative approach that combines semi-supervised inter-domain loss penalties to develop an end-to-end automatic speech recognition system. The inter-domain loss penalty, initially used in inter-domain speech synthesis, is adapted here for speech recognition and demonstrates improved performance on the WSJ, Librispeech, TIMIT, and TED-LIUM datasets, particularly in low-snr conditions. Our study compares different inter-domain loss penalties, including adversarial, cycle-consistency, and cycleGAN approaches, and finds that the latter yields state-of-the-art results on the WSJ dataset. Furthermore, we investigate the effect of varying cycleGAN hyperparameters and find that the best performance is often achieved with suboptimal visual-quality cycleGAN translations. Finally, we examine the importance of using same-domain training data and find that its omission can significantly degrade performance in low-snr conditions. The proposed approach is found to be robust to low signal quality and is therefore a valuable solution for speech recognition in adverse conditions. To investigate the influence of internal soft-molecule mobility on the Soret effect, we developed a theoretical model that considers rotational and vibrational motions. Using the multi-domain lattice model, we calculated the Soret effect for polyatomic molecules and molecules with double bonds. We discovered that in polyatomic molecules, rotational movement significantly contributes to the Soret effect, whereas vibrational motion has a negligible impact. Conversely, in molecules with double bonds, vibrational motion becomes more important and ultimately dominant. This understanding highlights the importance of distinguishing between different types of molecular movement when analyzing the Soret effect. Moreover, our research suggests that the Soret effect could serve as a diagnostic tool to investigate molecular movement within experimental studies of polyatomic and diatomic molecules. Lastly, we explored the Soret effect in chiral molecules, revealing that the total Soret effect is essentially zero due to the balanced contributions from right- and left-handed molecular movements. Nonetheless, it is theoretically feasible to observe non-zero Soret coefficients for molecules of specific handedness by examining their sum or difference. This finding presents an opportunity to utilize Soret coefficients as a means of detecting molecular chirality at a molecular level. Ultimately, our research aims to facilitate a deeper understanding of thermal diffusion phenomena in diverse molecular systems. Virtual human characters created through simulation are prone to inaccuracies when performing complex actions like throwing objects. This issue can be addressed by developing more realistic and understandable throwing motions, even if the simulation is imperfect. Our research focuses on the effects of simulated characters generating faux throwing motions with incorrect points of release, which are observable at the joint level. We discovered three primary consequences: the motion timing changes, resulting motion, and appearance of the motion. We employed two techniques to detect which type of throwing motion (faux or authentic) a simulated character should perform. Our results show that classifying faux throwing motions solely based on the timing is insufficient, as timing explains only 20% of the variance. Conversely, a combination of timing and motion path correlation explains about 40% of the variance. Ultimately, our research aims to contribute to the development of more realistic and understandable simulated human throwing motions. This paper presents new insights that can aid researchers in generating more authentic movements and developing more accurate classification methods for discrete faux throwing motion types. Furthermore, our research has significant implications for the fields of policy learning and goal-oriented reinforcement learning in simulation environments. A novel parsing-decoding method is proposed for neural machine translation based on a syntactic framework that starts from the top of the parse tree. This new approach differs from existing methods by modeling translation in a top-down manner similar to the shift-reduce algorithm used in sequence-to-sequence translation. To achieve this, a top-down parsing algorithm is employed to generate partial parse trees from leaves to roots based on analysis of sentence words and their associated syntactic links. Each partial parse tree is then used to derive translation probabilities from the trained neural model of syntactic decoders. Ultimately, the most likely translation is determined by choosing the highest-scoring final parse tree among all top-down parsing candidates. To expedite computation, a module is introduced to bypass unnecessary parsing candidates during the search process. In medical image analysis, particularly in diagnosis, image segmentation plays a pivotal role. However, due to the intricacies of medical imaging and the need for precise and accurate results, this process can be quite challenging. The use of deep learning models like U-Net, in conjunction with large annotated datasets, has made medical image segmentation more manageable. Nevertheless, these datasets often prove to be the primary constraint on implementing fully automated clinical workflows. The issue lies with the extensive resources needed to collect and label high-quality imaging data, a task more labor-intensive and costly than the training of the models themselves. To mitigate this problem, this research investigates whether image pre-processing techniques can help minimize the necessity for extensive annotation in medical image segmentation. To this end, several image enhancement methods, including standard normalization, color correction, and LANS, were applied to chest X-ray images, resulting in the significant reduction of the ground truth size by 90% without compromising segmentation accuracy. The experiments also show that combining these methods with LANS yields the best outcomes, underscoring its value as a data augmentation strategy, and its potential to be used as a tool to identify areas requiring more precise segmentation. The study's findings suggest that, under certain conditions, image pre-processing can serve as an effective alternative to reduce the necessity for extensive annotation in medical image segmentation tasks. Recent advancements in end-to-end neural speech-to-speech translation have shown significant progress despite the limitations of existing methods. These limitations become more pronounced in the area of zero-shot speech-to-speech translation that doesn't rely on language knowledge during training. Existing zero-shot methods typically rely on additional data or processing steps which can be difficult to deploy in practice. In this research, we investigate the possibility of developing a zero-shot speech-to-speech translation system directly from speech without requiring additional steps or intermediate representations. A major hurdle in this area stems from the fact that speech is a sequential signal. We propose a new approach that combines zero-shot speech-to-speech translation and zero-shot speech recognition into a single, unified model. This model is trained on speech features that are sequentially generated during training, allowing it to predict a sequence of vectors that encodes not only the source language sequence but also the source phonemes sequence. We present an implementation of this idea and show that it achieves competitive results on the WSJ, Librispeech, TED datasets and the OPUS dataset in zero-shot scenarios. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach outperforms state-of-the-art models in terms of translation accuracy. A thorough ablation study is also performed to examine the effect of various factors on the performance of the model. We believe that this work represents an important step towards developing a single, unified model for zero-shot speech-to-speech translation. This work extends the work on generalized heat conduction by modifying it to include dynamic boundary conditions and then derives unique boundary reconstruction methods for function and measure data on the boundary, also exploring the well-posedness of related operator equations. Furthermore, we establish a key result on the optimal continuous dependence of solutions on boundary data. The models and results are then applied to study a generalized heat conduction problem with a nonlinear heat transfer term and dynamic boundary conditions involving memory and sources. A thorough analysis of such problems with non-penalizing boundary conditions, lacking classical solutions, is provided in the paper. The results also show that even with a smoothing heat transfer term, smooth solutions may not exist, and instead we obtain weak and strong solutions in $L^2(0,T;H^{-1})$ and $L^2(0,T;H^{-3})$ respectively, and we further establish their continuous dependence on boundary data. Finally, we apply these results to study the long-time behavior of semidiscrete operator equations, and using compactness arguments, we prove the existence of global attractors for the complete problem with dynamic boundary conditions. The results provide a link between generalized heat conduction and memory-type heat conduction, and show that the latter can be viewed as a special case of the former when a smoothing operator is applied to the boundary equation of state. A novel vertebral body recognition method in CT scans is introduced, which combines image processing techniques with anatomical constraints. This approach begins with identifying vertebrae L1-L5 in the lumbar spine using a user-defined template, and employs a rectification method to correct spinal alignment, ensuring vertebrae remain stationary while surrounding organs move. Next, vertebral body centroids are estimated in lumbar and thoracic regions, and a constrained optimization algorithm localizes the vertebrae L5 to T12 by anchoring on centroids and adjusting translation and rotation. Finally, 3D reconstruction of vertebral bodies is performed in lumbar and thoracic regions. This method's adaptability and accuracy allow it to operate effectively in diverse spinal alignment configurations and detect even minor spinal fractures, demonstrating performance comparable to expert manual readings. Evaluations across 100 CT scans demonstrate high precision and robustness, with an average error of less than 1mm in 3D localization and a success rate of 98% in detecting fractures. This method's rapid processing speed and minimal interaction with image parameters make it an ideal solution for automated fracture detection and spinal reconstruction. A demonstration software, available for free download at https://sites.google.com/view/spine-automation/, enables users to easily integrate this technique into their workflow. This research paper presents a novel method for teaching a quadruped robot to move using elastic actuators in its legs. These actuators, also known as'series elastic actuators,' or SEAs, offer several benefits, including reduced wear and tear on the moving parts and improved resistance to damage. However, they make it more difficult for the control system to determine the position of the moving part. To address this problem, we developed a method that utilizes data from the entire system to predict its position. This prediction is then used to create a control system model that can be trained using a technique called 'policy gradient.' When tested, the system model demonstrated significant improvements in its ability to navigate a challenging terrain compared to a basic 'bang-bang' control system. In addition to better navigation skills, SEA-based robots also showed reduced peak forces and more efficient use of energy. This suggests that while data-driven methods may require more energy to operate, they offer several advantages when it comes to long-term system design.
