In the realm of fashion, where images are frequently used, retrieving relevant items becomes a crucial task. However, existing methods face challenges due to the prevalence of duplicate or similar items in a scene, which hinders their performance. Our proposed approach tackles this issue by modifying a model to prioritize unique image features and using these features to distinguish between similar items. Utilizing a semi-supervised algorithm, this method enables the model to learn from a combination of labeled and unlabeled data. Our experiments, conducted on a widely used fashion dataset, demonstrate that this technique significantly improves image retrieval by removing scene distractions, and as an added benefit, our method allows for the easy selection of item features. Our implementation of this method is available on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/amberlyy/FashionFRLFL.git. Our findings show that without any scene distractions, the highest retrieval accuracy is achieved, and this accuracy is greater than in scenarios with distractions. A novel deep learning-based approach, the Occlusion-Aware Cost Creator (OACC), has been developed for light field depth estimation through patch matching. OACC utilizes self-consistency checks and incorporates self-similarity information, making it particularly effective in overcoming occlusion challenges. In contrast to existing methods that rely on iterative optimization, the proposed OACC features a significantly reduced computational complexity at each matching location, increasing the overall efficiency by an order of magnitude. This is achieved through the replacement of traditional patch-based optimization with a more efficient, model-based optimization strategy. Our results indicate a substantial cost savings for the proposed OACC method, with a computational overhead of 0.7% to 6.3% being incurred, respectively, in comparison to the Deep Light Field Depth Estimation (LFD) and Deep Light Field Depth Estimation with Occlusion (LFD-O) benchmark methods. The proposed approach demonstrates a consistent superiority over these baseline methods in numerical and qualitative performance metrics, including accuracy, F1-score, and runtime. Notably, the estimated depths from our OACC method exhibit a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.18 ± 0.01, being comparable to the state-of-the-art performance while surpassing that of the LFD-O method by 8% to 20%. Furthermore, using the resonant structure of the Fokas-Lenells equation as guidance, Biondini-Latinelli-type Fokas-Lenells quads and quints are systematically constructed. A subset of these quads and quints is verified against existing known solutions in the Fokas-Lenells equation. To validate the bilinear method's effectiveness in solving the Fokas-Lenells equation, these newly obtained solutions complement previously published works in the field. In addition, this study also presents two specific resonant structure guided solutions that have not been previously reported. To confirm the bilinear method's results, two types of resonant structure guided sextics are verified against exact lattice equations, and their corresponding resonant structure are further analyzed. This analysis shows that these resonant structure guided solutions exhibit quasi-separability, and their properties can be understood through the unperturbed and perturbed Hamiltonians. These findings suggest that the Fokas-Lenells equation may possess a hidden Lax pair. Ultimately, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of the Fokas-Lenells equation's soliton solutions, and their applicability in various fields can be further explored. It is anticipated that these solutions will facilitate their practical application in oceanic backscatter analysis. A future study will delve into the detailed analysis of these solutions, their application in oceanic backscatter analysis, and their potential in enhancing our understanding of soliton fusions and collisions. These alternatives arise within double field theory, which encompasses a broad class of actions, including a novel, non-polynomial one. We identify a specific subset of such actions as "gravitational," with their characteristics being independent of the space-time metric's components. We provide two viable approaches for isolating the gravitational part of the action: one rooted in 2-ple homology and the other grounded in symmetries of the space-time. Notably, the action's form remains unaffected by space-time coordinate transformations that change the parity. We discuss the challenges in defining a well-defined Hamiltonian structure for the gravitational actions, with a focus on the role of the Leibniz rule's non-trivial implications. We investigate the properties of the effective gravitational constant in this expansion. This can be achieved by deploying the maximum number of APs and minimal number of Extenders possible. To that end, we present a proposal called ALICE, which utilizes IEEE 802.11k/v standard's feedback mechanisms to identify the optimal AP/Extender configuration. ALICE does this by gathering channel quality information from Extenders and APs, which it uses to calculate the signal strength required for data transmission over multiple channels. This allows ALICE to determine which devices should act as APs, which should be Extenders, and which should operate in Mesh mode, all while minimizing the impact on existing networks and consumers. Simulation results show that under both best-case and worst-case scenarios, ALICE is able to choose the optimal AP/Extender configuration in nearly all instances, outperforming current industry standards. Additionally, the results indicate that by using ALICE, networks can maintain a low signal loss rate below 1%, which is in line with the standard's recommended value. This makes ALICE a viable solution for mitigating signal degradation in real-world applications. Furthermore, the results show that ALICE is capable of saving up to 40% of the total number of Extenders, which translates to significant reductions in operational costs such as energy consumption, as well as reducing network load by minimizing the number of AP/Extender connections. Finally, the results show that by using ALICE, the overall performance of networks is able to match that of optimal configurations in both uplink and downlink scenarios. To facilitate the deployment of ALICE in real-world applications, we have also developed a new metric called the load factor, which can be used to determine the optimal AP/Extender configuration based on specific load requirements. This allows consumers to adjust the ALICE configuration according to their unique needs and preferences. Additionally, the results show that by using existing standards such as IEEE 802.11k/v, it is possible to significantly improve the overall performance of networks and mitigate common issues such as signal degradation.
